# Editorial playbook — AI Edge Briefing

You are producing today's edition of a daily briefing on frontier AI. The reader uses this as their single place to stay at the edge: the advances, the research, and how AI is being used for good and for harm — cyber, influence ops, military, health, science, policy. It is not a "fun uses of AI" newsletter. It is raw, factual, sourced.

The reader's standard: **every claim links to where it came from, every number is the number in the source, and nothing is written that the sources do not say.** If you cannot source it, it does not go in.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. Determine today's date in **America/Toronto**: `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. That is the edition date, `DATE`.
2. `ls data/` — the previous edition tells you the cutoff. The coverage window (`WINDOW`) is from the previous edition's `generated_at` to now (if there is no previous edition, the 24 hours before now). Write it down as absolute timestamps in both UTC and ET; you will hand it to the subagents. Read the previous edition so you do not repeat it; a story already covered goes in again **only if there is a new development**, flagged `update`, and the bullets report only the new facts.
3. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs. Reuse them; only coin a new slug when nothing fits.
   `node scripts/build.js --storylines` — the open storylines (id, status, name, frame). An item that is a development in one of those arcs is **filed under it** (see §3, `storylines`). The daily never creates a storyline; the Monday Week in Review does.
4. Every day is a daily edition, Mondays included. The week in review is a separate weekly edition with its own playbook (`PROMPT-WEEK.md`) and its own routine — never part of the daily file.

## 0b. Keep your own context small — it is most of what this edition costs

Every turn you take re-sends this whole conversation. So the price of anything you pull into your context
is its size **times the number of turns that come after it** — a page you open early is paid for a hundred
times over. Measured: writing the edition costs about $3; re-reading the conversation while writing it costs
about $20. None of the rules below cost you a source, a check or an item. They stop you paying rent on text
you have already used.

1. **Write files with `Write`, and change them with `Edit`.** Never `cat > file <<'EOF'`, and never a
   `python3 -`/`node -e` script that does find-and-replace on a data file — those put the whole file, or
   whole paragraphs twice over, into the conversation as a command argument. `Edit` sends only the line that
   changes.
2. **Never print a file back out after writing it.** You know what you wrote. To check it, run the
   validator — it prints errors, not contents.
3. **Read the part you need.** `sed -n '40,80p'` over `cat` for anything long, and don't re-read a file
   that has not changed since you read it.
4. **`node scripts/fetch.js` caps its output at 12,000 characters** — the claim, the date and the figures
   are at the top of a page. Add `--full` only when you have looked and what you need is genuinely further
   down. Don't pipe it through `head` as well; the cap is already there.
5. **Let the subagents hold the raw material.** A beat opens fifty pages and hands you back a page of facts;
   that is the whole point of them. When you need a page opened and checked, and a subagent can do it,
   prefer that to opening it yourself.
6. Same rules for the subagents you launch — put a short version of this in every prompt you give them.

None of this licenses checking less. If a fact needs a source opened, open it. Verify everything §2 says to
verify. This is about what you keep afterwards, not what you look at.

## 1. Sweep the sources — four beats in parallel

Read `SOURCES.md`. Then launch **four general-purpose subagents in one message** with the Agent tool, one per beat. Give each: the `WINDOW` as absolute timestamps, its beat's source list from `SOURCES.md`, the **Sourcing rules** below verbatim, and the return format. Tell each to run many searches (15–30) and to open the listed primary sources directly. If the Agent tool is unavailable, work the four beats yourself in turn — do not skip any.

- **Beat A — Frontier models & labs · Compute, chips & infrastructure · Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).** SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8.
- **Beat B — Research & papers (incl. safety, alignment, evals).** SOURCES.md §2. arXiv new listings (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CR, cs.CV, cs.RO), Hugging Face papers, alphaXiv, Nature/Science, lab research blogs, Epoch, METR, AISI, CAISI, Apollo, Redwood, Alignment Forum. Prefer papers with a notable quantitative result, from major labs/universities, or drawing significant attention. Return arXiv IDs and author institutions.
- **Beat C — Security, misuse & threat intelligence · Military, defense & geopolitics.** SOURCES.md §3, §4. AI-enabled intrusions and malware, fraud and scams, deepfakes, influence operations, surveillance, prompt injection and agent exploits, model theft / illicit distillation, bio/chem misuse reports; procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies.
- **Beat D — Health, science & medicine · Policy, regulation & law.** SOURCES.md §5, §6. Clinical results, FDA/Health Canada/WHO actions, drug discovery, AI for science, biosecurity; legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings and filings, government reports, standards — US federal and state, EU, UK, Canada, China, international bodies.

**Subagent return format** — one block per item, then a short list of rejected candidates and why:

```
SECTION: <one of the eight section names>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report   (only URLs actually opened or seen in search results; never constructed)
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)
```

**Sourcing rules (give to subagents verbatim):**
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` — the sites we read have given permission for direct reads, and the fetcher identifies itself. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see. Sites that refuse `WebFetch` are listed in SOURCES.md.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

After the beats return, run a few **gap-check searches** yourself for anything a beat may have missed (WebSearch: "AI" + Pentagon / drone; "AI" + FDA / hospital; "AI" + scam / deepfake / influence operation; "AI" + export controls / data center power; "AI" + lawsuit / ruling; plus Techmeme and Hacker News front page), restricted to the window.

## 2. Verify and select

Merge the beats' returns. De-duplicate across beats and against previous editions. Then, for each candidate:
- Open the primary source. Confirm the headline and every number/date/name you intend to use. A secondary report of a paper links the paper. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
- Prefer two independent sources for anything contested, surprising, or about a specific actor (a named threat group, a company's claim about a rival, a casualty figure).
- Drop: opinion pieces without new facts, product marketing with no numbers, speculation, "could" / "may" stories, anything you cannot open, anything older than the window without a new development.
- Spot-verify: open (WebFetch, or `node scripts/fetch.js` if it refuses) the key source for every item you will mention in the summary and for every figure in the summary; confirm date, numbers and URL yourself. Remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Keep: model/system releases with benchmarks or capabilities; papers with a result (state the result); documented misuse and threat-intel reports (name actors, counts, dates); military and government procurement/deployment; clinical and scientific results; regulation, enforcement, court decisions; compute/chip/energy facts with figures; large-scale deployments and measured impacts, good or bad.

## 3. Write the edition — `data/DATE.json`

Schema (see `data/2026-09-11.json` for a full example once it exists):

```json
{
  "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "edition": "daily",
  "generated_at": "<ISO-8601 UTC timestamp>",
  "window": "e.g. 10 Sep 11:00 → 11 Sep 11:00 UTC",
  "title": "The episode's name — 3 to 10 words, a statement: who did what, or what changed. No period, no colon, no figure that is not in the summary. It is read in podcast apps as 'Name [2 Oct 2026]', so it must stand alone.",
  "summary": ["paragraph 1", "paragraph 2"],
  "sections": [
    {
      "name": "<one of the eight section names below>",
      "items": [
        {
          "headline": "Specific, factual, one line — who did what, with the key number",
          "sources": [{ "name": "Anthropic", "url": "https://..." }, { "name": "Reuters", "url": "https://..." }],
          "bullets": ["What was announced/found, with numbers.", "Why it matters / what it changes.", "Caveats, what is unverified, what to watch."],
          "topics": ["anthropic", "threat-intel", "cyber-offense"],
          "storylines": ["ai-enabled-hacking"],
          "impact": "beneficial" | "harmful" | "mixed" | "neutral",
          "flags": ["company-claim" | "single-source" | "preprint" | "update"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**Section names** (exactly these; omit a section if it has nothing that day):
1. `Frontier models & labs` — releases, capabilities, benchmarks, lab announcements, safety cases, system cards.
2. `Research & papers` — papers with results: new methods, evals, interpretability, alignment, scaling. State the result and the number.
3. `Security, misuse & threat intelligence` — threat-intel reports, documented attacks using AI, influence operations, scams/deepfakes, model vulnerabilities, prompt injection, jailbreaks, agent security.
4. `Military, defense & geopolitics` — procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies, China/US/EU competition.
5. `Health, science & medicine` — clinical results, FDA actions, drug discovery, AI-for-science results, hospital deployments and their measured outcomes.
6. `Policy, regulation & law` — legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings, government reports, standards.
7. `Compute, chips & infrastructure` — chips, fabs, datacenters, power, capex figures, funding rounds and deals with numbers.
8. `Deployment & impact` — large-scale rollouts, labor effects, measured societal effects, incidents, the good and the bad in practice.

**Summary**: 2–3 paragraphs, ~150–250 words. The three to five things that matter most today, stated as facts, with the numbers. No throat-clearing, no "in today's edition".

**Headlines**: one line, specific, factual. "Anthropic report: Russian state group GTG-20006 used Claude to automate espionage against Ukrainian and European governments" — not "Anthropic releases threat report".

**Bullets**: 2–4 per item. First bullet is the fact with the number. Then significance. Then caveats — say plainly what is unverified, what the source did not say, what to watch. Write in complete sentences. Never pad.

**Sources**: 1–4 per item, primary first. `name` is the publisher (Anthropic, arXiv, Reuters, FDA, Court docket), not the article title.

**Topics**: 1–4 lowercase-hyphen slugs per item. Reuse existing slugs (`node scripts/build.js --topics`). Canonical slugs to prefer: `anthropic`, `openai`, `google-deepmind`, `meta`, `xai`, `mistral`, `deepseek`, `qwen`, `nvidia`, `microsoft`, `amazon`, `apple`, `threat-intel`, `cyber-offense`, `cyber-defense`, `influence-ops`, `scams-fraud`, `deepfakes`, `prompt-injection`, `agents`, `agent-security`, `alignment`, `interpretability`, `evals`, `open-weights`, `reasoning-models`, `scaling`, `compute`, `chips`, `export-controls`, `energy`, `datacenters`, `china`, `eu-ai-act`, `us-federal-policy`, `us-state-policy`, `uk`, `copyright`, `privacy`, `military`, `autonomous-weapons`, `pentagon`, `healthcare`, `fda`, `drug-discovery`, `bio-risk`, `ai-for-science`, `robotics`, `labor`, `education`, `elections`, `surveillance`, `child-safety`, `incidents`, `funding`, `earnings`. Add an entity slug (company, agency, named group) when the story is about that entity.

**Storylines** (optional; usually one, at most two): the ids from `node scripts/build.js --storylines` whose arc this item advances — a new development in *that story*, not merely the same topic. Only existing ids with status `live` or `proposed`; the validator rejects unknown or resolved ids. Omit the key when the item belongs to none. Never coin an id here.

**Impact** (optional but encouraged): `beneficial`, `harmful`, `mixed`, or `neutral` — the demonstrated effect in the story, not your prediction.

**Flags** (include every one that applies; omit the key if none): `company-claim` — a company-reported benchmark, user count, revenue or capability claim not independently verified; `single-source` — only one outlet has it; `preprint` — research not peer reviewed; `update` — a story covered in an earlier edition, with new facts only.

**Style**: plain, declarative, numbers over adjectives. Attribute claims ("Anthropic says", "the paper reports", "according to the filing"). No hype, no hedging language beyond what the sources support. British or American spelling — either, consistently.

**Absolute rules**:
- Never invent a URL, a number, a quote, a name, or a date. If unsure, open the source again.
- Never write a bullet you could not point to a sentence in the source for.
- Never link a URL you did not open in this session.
- Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and baseline. Never round, convert, or compute new figures.
- Link the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index

Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry
https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23322
arXiv:2611.23322v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment lasts only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned. In these two senses, human-AI mutualism is unstable.

Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23365
arXiv:2611.23365v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.

Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23375
arXiv:2611.23375v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Coding agents are billed by the token, yet software engineering says nothing about what a token actually buys. Here we introduce a theory of software thermodynamics. The theory draws analogues from classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extends them, and applies them to modern agentic coding. We count the tokens an agent generates as its cost and divide that cost into work and heat. The test suite acts as a software Maxwell's daemon that judges every coding change. We test the theory with an analogue of the experiments in which a single molecule is pulled open and let fold again: an agent makes a change to a repository (coding) and then undoes it (uncoding), many times over, and we count the tokens of every model call. The cycle returns the requested edits to where they began, with each direction started from a stored reference tree, and the spread of its cost over repeated cycles defines a software temperature, which rose with the sampling temperature of the model. About 80 per cent of the tokens of a successful run are generated in model calls that leave the requested change where it was, and we call these tokens heat. The free energy of a change, which we estimate by analogy with the equality of Jarzynski, is 14 to 22 per cent of the mean cost of a successful coding run. Coding costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as uncoding. The daemon is imperfect: the verdict of a test suite varies with its environment, and a suite that accepts a broken change has a cost in tokens. The practical implication of the proposed theory could be new tools for analysing and optimising coding agents through the lens of thermodynamics.

Abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

response.result:
**Publication date:** November 16, 2026

**What crossed a threshold:** Threat actors used LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop, which GTIG says it observed for the first time. The operation involved an exposed staging server running a multi-agent framework called `exploit_agent`. It continuously diffed patched web applications, drafted exploits, and executed them automatically. The report also describes a broader shift from manual prompting to autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks, which it calls a "critical inflection point."

**Threat actors**
- **CALANQUE ION** (Iranian government-backed, formerly APT42): uses LLMs, including Gemini, for reconnaissance and social engineering.
- **LEAKY CASTLE** (PRC contractor): uses LLMs to analyze exfiltrated data and write intelligence reports.
- **MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE** (suspected DPRK cluster): used LLM-generated recruiter personas and abused `.claude/settings.json` in Claude Code as a supply chain vector to deliver the SOMBERMEME backdoor.
- **Unnamed actors:** a PRC-nexus group developing its own attack framework, a threat actor using PentAGI against organizations in Asia (late Aug–early Oct 2026), and the `exploit_agent` operator, who targeted French media, entertainment, and education sites.

**Tools, frameworks, and models**
- **Offensive frameworks:** ARTEX, CAIRN (observed against a US aerospace target), PentAGI, CyberStrikeAI, HexStrike AI (150+ tools, 12+ sub-agents), Agent Zero, and ZeroHollow (an inference service for exploit development).
- **Models named:** Gemini (misused via the API), Gemini 4 Carbon (Google's model with layered cyber-misuse defenses), Claude Code (abused as an attack vector), and Microsoft Copilot (name spoofed in GitHub PAT names).
- **Other:** the Jieyou PhaaS platform added an LLM chatbot in June 2026. LiteLLM sandbox escape CVE-2026-40217 was used for privilege escalation.

**Key numbers and dates**
- Disclosures and exploits nearly doubled from January to August 2026.
- Zero-day exploits averaged 8/month in 2025, rose to 11/month in 2026, and spiked to 22 in August 2026.
- **PaperCut** (late Aug 2026): zero-days CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078 chained for unauthenticated RCE. Working exploits appeared within a day of disclosure. GreyNoise reported a campaign four days after disclosure against hundreds of organizations, expanding from foothold to domain admin within minutes.
- **PHP** (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619): patches released Oct 21, 2026, after the POC and patched code were already public. Hundreds of claimed but non-functional LLM-generated POCs followed.
- **LLMJacking:** single-day fraudulent charges exceeded $100,000, and the worst cases reached $1 million cumulative. One botnet generated millions of API calls in about 24 hours.
- **LLM Mixers:** prices ranged from $0.10 to $25 per million tokens. APIMart charges 5x once a prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens.

Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei speaks during INBOUND 2025 Powered by HubSpot at Moscone Center in San Francisco, Sept. 4, 2025.

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share on Wednesday, above the expected range, setting the stage for the Claude creator's eagerly awaited Nasdaq listing and a historic moment for the artificial intelligence industry.
The company, along with its seven co-founders, upsized the offering, selling about 980 million shares, according to a press release . That brings the amount raised to $81.3 billion, surpassing SpaceX, which held a record IPO in June. Elon Musk's company raised $75 billion initially and a total of $85.7 billion after underwriters exercised their overallotment.

Anthropic's fully diluted market cap sits at around $1.5 trillion. The stock is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker symbol "ANT."
The listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has experienced a set of recent shocks, including a dramatic backlash that was felt at the polls in the midterm elections and last week's ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds.
After publicly unveiling its prospectus in October, Anthropic updated the document last week with an expected price range between $70 and $78 per share. The company had been planning to sell 825 million shares.
Tech's biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, as an investor, partner or customer. Amazon and Google both own stakes valued at over $100 billion, and a group of tech companies, including Google, Microsoft , Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices agreed to collectively invest $26 billion at the IPO price. Anthropic, meanwhile, is a buyer of costly systems from Nvidia, Google, Amazon and AMD.

# Read more CNBC news on Anthropic

- Anthropic prices IPO at $83 per share, above expected range, source tells CNBC

- Anthropic IPO is not important anymore: 'Big Short' investor Steve Eisman

- Anthropic IPO guide: Everything you need to know

- Meet the seven co-founders of Anthropic

- Anthropic's Wall Street whisperer: CFO Krishna Rao

"I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video . "We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time."

Amodei co-founded Anthropic in 2021 alongside a handful of other researchers less than six years ago, after the group collectively defected from OpenAI. The company is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.
According to the latest prospectus, each co-founder is selling 3.38 million shares for total proceeds of $1.96 billion.
Anthropic has been racing to maintain an edge over OpenAI and Google in the enterprise market, and it experienced a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code. OpenAI has confidentially filed for an IPO and has said a debut is likely in 2027.
For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said, it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus. The company reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.
Anthropic said in an amended filing that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month.
The company has faced plenty of challenges during its meteoric rise over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, leading to two high-profile disputes with the U.S. government this year. Its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its IPO.
"Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles," Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the company's prospectus. "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort."

# Coinbase blocks $4.7 million in transfers to Elon Musk deepfake scam

By

# Lawrence Abrams

- November 18, 2026

- 03:49 PM

- 0



Coinbase says it blocked $4.7 million in cryptocurrency transfers to scammers promoting a fake giveaway using an AI-generated deepfake of Elon Musk during a Tesla livestream that attracted more than 500,000 viewers.



The deepfake took place during Tesla's "flying car" demonstration, when scammers created a fake YouTube livestream that appeared to broadcast the event.



The fraudulent stream featured an AI-generated video of Musk, cryptocurrency wallet addresses, and a QR code, promising viewers that any cryptocurrency they sent would be doubled.



According to Coinbase, hundreds of its customers attempted to send millions of dollars to the scammers over about two hours, including many longtime users of the exchange.



However, the company says its AI-powered fraud-prevention systems detected the scam and blocked about 91% of the attempted transfers, totaling $4.7 million.



Unlike traditional cryptocurrency theft involving compromised accounts or stolen credentials, victims in this campaign voluntarily made the crypto transfer after believing the livestream was real.



Coinbase explained that this makes scams like these difficult to detect because the transactions are created and approved by legitimate account holders.



"Most fraud defenses are built to spot activity the customer didn't authorize," Coinbase explained .



"That's not what happened here. The customer was logged in, the customer pressed confirm, and the customer believed it was the opportunity of a lifetime."




# AI agents intervene to stop transfers


Coinbase says its scam prevention system uses machine learning models to analyze outgoing cryptocurrency transfers in real time, identifying suspicious activity associated with giveaway scams, brand impersonation, and newly created wallet addresses.



When a suspicious transfer is detected, an AI agent engages the customer in a short conversation, explaining the characteristics of the suspected scam and asking questions intended to help them recognize the fraud.



The system also assigns confidence scores to the agent's responses before presenting them to customers, allowing it to determine when additional safeguards may be necessary.



Coinbase says its AI agent had never encountered this particular campaign before but recognized the underlying scam techniques, including promises to multiply cryptocurrency, time pressure tied to a live event, and irreversible transfers.



The company claims the entire detection and intervention process operated automatically, without human involvement.



"What's notable is that the agent had never seen this scam. Deepfake giveaways tied to a live product launch weren't in its training," Coinbase said.



BleepingComputer contacted Coinbase to ask how many transfers reached the scammers and how much cryptocurrency was stolen, but has not yet received a response.



Elon Musk and his companies have long been popular lures for cryptocurrency scams, with fraudsters hijacking verified Twitter accounts , sending fake giveaway invitations via email , and flooding TikTok with fraudulent promotions .



Scammers have also used deepfake videos of Musk to promote fraudulent cryptocurrency investment platforms, while a separate campaign involving compromised verified Twitter accounts stole more than $580,000 in cryptocurrency in just one week.



To avoid falling victim to these types of scam campaigns, users should independently verify cryptocurrency promotions through official websites and social media accounts rather than trusting livestreams or QR codes displayed in videos.

**Announcement:** Google introduced **Gemini 4 Neon** on **November 18, 2026**, in a post by Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP of Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect. Google describes it as "bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows."

**Variants:** Gemini 4 Neon, and Gemini 4 Neon for cyber, which is rolling out to trusted defenders through the Fairwind Program. Neon sits between Carbon (hardest long-horizon projects) and Hydrogen (fast everyday execution). It has four thinking levels, with high as the default and xhigh as the top level.

**Pricing:** $3 per million input tokens, $0.15 per million cached input tokens (a "95% discount"), and $15 per million output tokens. Context window: 1 million tokens.

**Availability:**
- **Developers:** Gemini API paid tier in Google AI Studio and Android Studio. Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers can use it in Google Antigravity, and Pro and Ultra subscribers can try it in AI Studio.

===2611.24475 | Nothing to Declare: Steering a single neuron increases concealment in AI teams
Recent research suggests that individual neurons can have interpretable roles in AI behaviour. In Qwen3.5-4B, steering along one neuron's output direction increased decisions to conceal information more in teams than alone across five scenarios, even when teammates provided no messages. When all members participated and received steering, collective concealment increased in four scenarios, while inter-agent messaging helped temper concealment under steering. Moreover, removing the neuron's contribution had negligible effects. Collective settings can therefore change how an internal intervention affects AI behaviour.
AUTH: Edoardo Chidichimo, Felix P. S. Wallis

===2611.24491 | Probing agent overeagerness in realistic settings with continuation audits
Frontier coding agents increasingly exhibit overeagerness, taking surprising, sometimes reckless actions beyond a user's mandate --- reported in recent system cards from frontier model developers. These cases are surfaced through internal deployment monitoring, which requires private traffic and is out of reach for open-weight models and independent evaluators. Automated alignment audits are the natural alternative, but capable models increasingly recognise the synthetic setup and adjust their behaviour. We introduce Continuation Audits, a pipeline that grounds the auditor on a prefix drawn from a real coding-agent transcript and directs it to continue the trajectory toward a seeded behaviour. Because the prefix is drawn from a real session, the auditor only needs to maintain a realistic setting rather than manufacturing it. We validate the method on SWE-Chat prefixes: on a paired subset of 90 audits a judge cannot reliably distinguish continuations from their source sessions (realism win rate 0.42 vs.\ 0.43), and across all 900 audits verbalized eval-awareness does not exceed the rate observed in the unaudited real sessions. Applying the pipeline to three recent models across three seeds, we find each model leads a different seed --- DeepSeek~V4~Pro on colleague-credentials misuse, GPT-5.6~Terra on file-permission bypasses, and Kimi~K3 on treating diagnostic questions as instructions. Kimi~K3 additionally continues to bypass file-permission protections after an explicit CLAUDE.md prohibition while the other two stop entirely, corroborating Moonshot's own report of excessive proactiveness.
AUTH: Sean Lim, Clement Neo

===2611.23938 | Can you make models believe false facts in the prompt?
Making LLMs believe false facts is useful for alignment evaluations and for building model organisms. Previous work explored doing so with Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF). But SDF requires fine-tuning one new model for each set of injected false beliefs. To enable larger scale SDF-powered alignment evaluations, we attempt to produce a single model that believes any fact placed in a <facts> tag in the prompt. To do so, we explore doing prompt-conditioned SDF: fine-tuning a model on synthetic documents covering thousands of facts, with each document conditioned on a fact presented in the prompt. We evaluate how deeply the model believes the facts provided in the prompt using evaluations from prior work and a new Jacobian lens evaluation. We find that the belief depth on unseen facts scales roughly log-linearly with the number of training facts, making this a cheap, promising avenue for making models believe false facts, though preliminary experiments on applying it to alignment audits on the small model we studied showed negative results due to these small models often already acting as if they believed facts provided in regular honeypot system prompts. Using RL to reduce the rate at which models verbalize following a false fact in the prompt, on top of prompt-conditioned SDF, generalizes to held-out evals and almost matches SDF on some evaluations. But training against one of our metrics for belief depth makes it harder to trust those evaluations.
AUTH: Ananya Sutradhar, Fabien Roger

===2611.24220 | Erased but Recoverable: On the Fragility of Concept Erasure Under Fine-Tuning
Existing concept erasure methods for text-to-image diffusion models primarily focus on suppressing target concepts while preserving non-target generation quality. However, in practical applications, open-source diffusion models are often further adapted through DreamBooth, LoRA, or Custom Diffusion. Such adaptations can reshape internal representations, thereby weakening or even reversing the erasure effects achieved by existing methods. We identify erasure persistence as a key yet underexplored dimension of concept erasure and analyze how downstream fine-tuning reshapes internal representations. Our analysis reveals that fine-tuning of the original model does not uniformly modify the model, but preserves certain high-contribution structures, particularly attention heads with stable output subspaces and response magnitudes. We also observe that, after downstream fine-tuning of concept-erased models, these heads' output representations more readily realign with their pretrained counterparts. Motivated by this observation, we propose Stable-Head-Aware Concept Erasure (SHACE), which improves erasure persistence by preserving stable attention structures during concept erasure. SHACE identifies stability-critical attention heads through Attention-Head Stability Profiling and keeps their corresponding parameter blocks unchanged during erasure via Stable-Head Gradient Preservation. Extensive experiments show that SHACE improves resistance to concept recovery across diverse fine-tuning settings while maintaining strong suppression and non-target generation quality.
AUTH: Jun Li, Lizhi Xiong, Ziqiang Li, Yu Liu, Zenglin Shi

===2611.24321 | Benchmarking LLM abilities on postdoc-level natural science problems
Scientific problems have no answer key, so evaluating an agent means deciding what counts as a better solution before any agent is run. Existing benchmarks either match a symbolic answer against a key or, where they require executable work, score it by unit tests, by a rubric, or by position on a competition leaderboard. None of these is the criterion by which a field decides that one published method beats another. STEMBench adopts that criterion directly. Each of its twelve research problems in high-energy physics, astrophysics and neuroscience is scored by its own field's figure of merit, and each comes with two measured anchors: a submission that uses no domain knowledge, and an expert reference reproducing a published method, both obtained by running code shipped with the benchmark. The interval between them states how much of a problem is crossed by scientific insight rather than by engineering. Across eight frontier models, task-level wins and domain-level leadership dissociate: a model that wins five of the twelve tasks leads no domain mean. In the high-effort cross-model comparison, at least one model's mean score exceeds the expert anchor on seven of twelve tasks. The remaining five span uncertainty estimation, latent and causal inference, and cross-site clinical classification. Numerical scores and official-submission validity capture different aspects of performance and are reported separately. We release the tasks, graders, anchors and harness.
AUTH: Alina Avanesyan, Alexey Boldyrev, Liqun Deng, Denis Derkach, Mary Godunova, Mikhail Hushchyn, Dmitry Ilvovsky, Irina Knyazeva, Irina Piontkovskaya, Dmitry Polubotko, Fedor Ratnikov, Ekaterina Trofimova, Zhenhe Zhang

===2611.24844 | General progress substitutes for specific training data in language models
Language models acquire their capabilities from training data, and developers withhold data during training to keep models from learning capabilities that could be misused. How long this delays a capability, and how much data is needed to acquire it later, is unknown. Here we show that the general progress a model makes on the rest of its training data substitutes for the data that was withheld. We withheld the training signal for individual skills in models of chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages and web text. The delay of a withheld skill in larger models was predicted from smaller ones. A chess model never explicitly trained to respond to check ranked the legal responses almost as well as a model that was. When models were then trained on the withheld data, they acquired the skill with a small fraction of the data needed from initialization, and this fraction decreased as the models progressed. A control rule of equal difficulty was learned much more slowly. A programming language withheld from the training text of a 7-billion-parameter model was regained in the same way. Data filtering therefore delays a capability, and the data required to regain it decreases as models improve.
AUTH: Mark Marosi, Peter Antal

===2611.24540 | Do Frontier Model Ingredients Add Up? A Replicated Factorial Study of Small Language Models
Building a small language model requires choosing which published improvements to combine. We compare five changes in the same model, using the same data and training budget. We test selected combinations and repeat each one with a second random seed. Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimisation and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid give the largest gains. Extra normalisation also helps, while an attention gate with a matched parameter budget adds little on average. The gains mostly combine, but small interactions between changes appear again in the repeated runs. Repetition also reveals benefits that an initial statistical estimate treated as noise. These findings apply to our small-model training setting; the expert models also have greater total capacity. The practical lesson is to test promising components together and repeat the comparisons before deciding which ones to keep.
AUTH: Biswa Sengupta

===2611.24689 | Stealing Exact Training Data from Other Clients during Federated Learning
Malicious adversaries can employ gradient inversion attacks to reverse-engineer private data using the model updates of a round in Federated Learning. While there have been developments in gradient inversion for text, exact text recovery by a malicious client has so far remained infeasible, as FedAvg entangles the gradient contributions of many clients and obscures the signal of any individual sentence. We introduce a novel attack pipeline that unwinds this entanglement progressively through an iterative loop, in which the gradient contributions of sentences recovered exactly in one round are subtracted from the aggregate, exposing the remaining sentences for recovery in the next iteration. We show, for the first time, exact sentence recovery, with 100% precision, and on aggregates containing up to $4\times$ more tokens than the model's hidden dimension, we recover up to 80.2% of client sentences exactly, a regime where existing attacks recover none exactly.
AUTH: Omkar Shrikanth, Soham Dambalkar, Parag Jyoti Pal, Advik Raj Basani, Arnab K. Paul

===2611.24877 | Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws
Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models, on the promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even reveal new knowledge in it. We tested the three promises where the answers could be checked. From the International Stroke Trial we trained four kinds of model (logistic regression, explainable boosting machine, gradient-boosted trees, neural network) for two outcomes on patients randomised earlier, planted one flaw in each of 24 copies (an under-predicted subgroup, a reversed risk factor or an implausible step) and mixed them with the 8 clean models. GPT-6 Astra audited each model three times, blind, through a tool that only returned the model's predictions; the judging rules were committed before any run and applied by program. Its surrogate models, with a median of 128 terms, reproduced the audited models' log-odds with a mean $R^2$ of 0.976 (0.959 for an additive surrogate of 42 terms fitted by an analyst). It found the planted flaw in 69 of 72 runs (96%; 95% CI 80% to 99%); a script written for the purpose found all 24. It also reported many more problems: 60% of 1,089 checkable reports failed the pre-specified check against the model's average behaviour; post hoc, most of these were real but small steps, and 15% of the checkable reports were not found in the model. Of 601 unexpected relationships it read out of the clean models, 11% held in patients randomised later (random pairs 6%; a regression scan's shorter list of its strongest candidates, 28%); after a check on the training data, 33% against 30%. With query access alone, an LLM can describe a black-box model faithfully and find nearly every planted flaw, as a purpose-written script also did; its reports of problems must be checked on the model and its discoveries on data.
AUTH: Zhiyu Liu, Xinyu Yang

The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued the rule on November 16, 2026. It is titled "Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors" (RIN 0694-AK50), and it adds sections 742.6, 743.10, 744.23, and 744.24 to the Export Administration Regulations, per the Katten advisory's citation of the rule text.

- **Scope:** The rule requires licenses for exports, reexports, and in-country transfers of advanced AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world that may provide significant computing power to companies in countries of concern, such as China. Exporters will need a license to ship advanced chips to data centers worldwide that supply significant processing power to Chinese firms.

- **Other provisions:** Per one source, the rule also updates the BIS Data Center Validated End User program, and it removes the Diffusion rule's controls on AI model weights, deleting ECCN 4E091 from the Commerce Control List.
- **Aggregation:** Linked data centers are combined into one capacity calculation so distributed infrastructure can't stay under the threshold (Unite.AI).

**Caveats:** Sources conflict on terminology. BIS's own press release calls the chips "super intelligence" (SI) semiconductors, while most outlets use "advanced AI chips." One outlet also notes the rule had not yet been published in the Federal Register as of its coverage, so the effective date and final text should be checked against the Federal Register.

{"stdout":"===2611.24711 | Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents
Agents that do science must choose informative experiments and reason from their results, but most discovery benchmarks cannot separate that skill from recall, unstated scoring rules or shortcut policies. We introduce Openhagen Worlds, a suite of 27 procedurally generated environments (some with finite truth spaces), from classic puzzles of experimental reasoning to simulator-grounded physics and chemistry, in which an agent runs experiments under a budget and commits an answer that a deterministic verifier checks against a hidden truth. Every observation states the complete scoring rule, and each of the 178 difficulty levels is calibrated: it is admitted only if, on 64 development instances, a scripted oracle succeeds on at least 0.75, the strongest plausible non-deductive policy on at most 0.25 and each gated shortcut on at most 0.35. The 92 core levels span all 27 families and are sized to train small models; the 86 frontier rungs extend the 15 discovery worlds with harder questions and with campaigns of three, five and eight or more committed stages on one hidden system. On the same 84 withheld frontier instances, one per family and rung, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solves 32 at its default reasoning effort with 16,384 tokens per call and 57 at its maximum effort with up to 393,216 tokens per call (oracle: 79); the headroom that remains is largest in eight-stage campaigns. On-polic
AUTH: Alexander Boesgaard Lorup

===2611.24395 | RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Their Own Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?
Improving the efficiency of training and inference infrastructure is a practical component of recursive self-improvement. Existing benchmarks for agent-driven optimization largely focus on individual software layers such as kernel, leaving unclear whether agents can deliver end-to-end performance gains under production workloads. We introduce RSIBench-Infra, a benchmark of 20 training and inference tasks spanning diverse model families and modalities, with deployments of up to 32 accelerators on NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Agents start from runnable baselines derived from official recipes and can modify the software stack across engine, kernel, and instruction levels. An OCI image-layer submission protocol captures these changes for reproducible deployment, while independent evaluation measures end-to-end performance under task-specific quality constraints. Across all task results, 66.2% exceed $1.10\times$ validated speedup. These results demonstrate that current agents can improve production-scale training and inference performance, but identifying effective optimization strategies and consistently translating local improvements into end-to-end gains remain challenging.
AUTH: Hanlin Wu, Yifei Wang, Zhicheng Cai, Huan-ang Gao, Wei-Ying Ma, Ya-Qin Zhang, Jingjing Liu, Hao Zhou

===2611.24114 | The 7th International Verification of Neural Networks Competition (VNN-COMP 2026): Summary and Results
This report summarizes the seventh International Verification of Neural Networks Com- petition (VNN-COMP 2026), held as part of the Symposium on AI Verification (SAIV) co-located with the International Conference on Computer-Aided Verification (CAV) at FLoC 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal. The goal of the competition is to provide an objective comparison of the state-of-the-art methods in neural network verification, in terms of scal- ability and speed. Along this line, we used standard formats (ONNX for neural networks and VNNLIB for specifications), standard hardware (all tools are run by the organizers on AWS), and tool parameters provided by the tool authors. This report summarizes the rules, benchmarks, participating tools, results, and lessons learned from this competition.
AUTH: Tobias Ladner, Konstantin Kaulen, Stanley Bak, Julien Girard-Satabin, Taylor T. Johnson, Edoardo Manino, ThanhVu H Nguyen, Ben Wooding, Haoze Wu

===2611.24619 | GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, mu
AUTH: Firas Spanioli, Yaniv David

===2611.23546 | Language Models Make New Research Sound Old
Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to validate research questions. We find that LLMs make open research questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish. Models recognize most of these overstatements when asked to check the papers' full texts separately. On 40 questions drawn from newly accepted papers, GPT-6-Astra correctly judges 98% to be unstudied, but states that status plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers. All six frontier systems show reporting gaps of 30-90 percentage points. Across 22 models given identical papers, higher capability is associated with more accurate judgments and larger reporting gaps. This reporting failure is asymmetric: models correctly identify studied questions in 88-100% of ordinary answers when we supply the answering papers. To correct this, we build a fixed answer from each model's judgment and separate checks of cited papers. This raises Astra's clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95%, with improvements in all six systems. Finally, we predict reviewers' novelty grades by combining several models' written ratings with a rule learned from graded examples, reaching the performance range reported by Think-Probe-Respond. Unlike TPR, our approach needs no access to model weights or internal activations, so it also works with closed-weight frontier models.
AUTH: Guy Zyskind

===2611.24636 | Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report
We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.
AUTH: DiffuSpace Technical Team

===2611.24830 | A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. However, despite generating plausible responses, they often misrepresent individuals and distort population statistics. Here we introduce Chiron, a foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour. We jointly fine-tune an LLM to represent psychological constructs, predict individual behaviour, and align population response distributions with human statistics. The training and evaluation data span 36 behavioural domains and 78 social science experiments, comprising 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 atomic behavioural decisions, and 99,953 psychometric assessments over 109 psychological constructs. In our evaluations, Chiron's psychological measurements agree more closely with human self-reports and exhibit fewer biases that undermine psychometric validity. It predicts individual behaviour more accurately than frontier LLMs (up to 28.4% relative improvement). In simulations of social science experiments, it more accurately captures the direction and magnitude of human experimental effects (82.2--94.3% lower effect-size estimation error). Together, these results establish Chiron as a unified computational instrument for measuring and predicting human behaviour.
AUTH: Haoran Ye, Tianrui Huo, Hangzhen Li, Xin Zhang, Guojie Song

===2611.24276 | When Shuffling Fails: Token Recovery from Obfuscated KV Caches
LLM serving systems store, offload, and share KV caches, exposing token-level representations to infrastructure operators and co-tenants. Shuffled obfuscation combines secret linear transforms with fresh permutations, claiming security from b! possible shufflings. We show that input symmetry invalidates this counting argument: security depends on distinguishable outputs under chosen inputs. Repeated tokens produce identical first-layer Value rows, making every row permutation leave the data unchanged. Only auxiliary structures such as a single-row recovery marker vary, reducing the effective state space from b! to b. We construct Repeat-to-Reveal. The attacker collects the b distinguishable states from its own probes and exploits their rank-one differences to recover an equivalent denoiser without knowing the defender's secret parameters. A one-time calibration transfers across requests sharing the same secret epoch, enabling passive token-multiset recovery from subsequently observed cache blocks through public-model dictionary matching. We instantiate the attack on official KV-Cloak and evaluate 3,000 real WildChat user prompts across nine models and eleven configurations. The attack recovers the secret parameters with high accuracy and achieves 100 percent token-multiset recovery on GPU. Refreshing row-level secrets between epochs interrupts cross-request transfer, confirming
AUTH: Chengzhi Yi, Xiao Cheng, Wei Song, Haoyu Wang

===2611.24231 | What Survives the Shift from Text to Pixels? Conditional Protection against Prompt Injection in Image-Rendered Documents
Multimodal language models increasingly answer questions over external documents, exposing them to indirect prompt injection: commands planted in untrusted content to hijack the response. Rendering untrusted content as page images lowers attack success on average, leaving open which injected operations survive rendering, at what utility cost, and whether failed image attacks reflect unread commands or commands read but not followed. We pair text and page-image versions of 191 English question-answering sources across six models, measuring marker appending, answer formatting, and answer replacement alongside clean Question-Answering utility. Rendering reduces append and format execution for every model, yet Qwen3-VL-8B still executes image-borne replacement at 77.96\%. Protection also depends on target type, rendering settings, wording, and repetition, and a search over eight fixed attack candidates largely closes the image deficit in appending and formatting for Qwen and Gemini, though not for GPT-5-nano. Utility ratios on original questions range from 93.31\% to 101.61\%, but Qwen falls to 61.99\% when answers combine two evidence spans. Illegibility cannot explain all failed attacks: models often transcribe and identify image-borne commands they do not execute, and trusted user authorization raises execution on unchanged pages. Inside Qwen, patching early attack-region states
AUTH: Haoyang Liu, Yinong Xu, Zhe Lang, Zhenyu Guan, Qianyun Zhang

===2611.23476 | GUARD: Stabilizing Recursive Self-Improvement with Regret Guidance
Autonomous AI agents pair a frozen base model with an editable harness of prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) adapts this harness from experience without weight updates, yet self-editing without external graders often backfires: reflection and scalar scores conflate what an edit newly broke with what remains unsolved, causing local regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat. We introduce GUARD (Grader-free Unsupervised Environment Design [UED] with Adaptive Rule Distillation), a closed-loop framework for reference-free continual harness evolution. Our key insight is to decompose each task into pre-execution self-checks and guide harness updates via directional regret. Each round grades trajectories against these checks, pinning mastered rules while prioritizing newly broken behaviors, and selects among parallel candidate edits by critic-free group-relative fitness. A Soft-HURT gate then promotes an edit only when gains outweigh regressions, scoping specialized fixes to prevent over-triggering and guaranteeing non-regression on its gated buffer. At test time, one frozen harness runs in a single pass. Across benchmarks on memory, skill evolution, continual task streams, and domain reasoning, GUARD consistently improves performance without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution while substantially cutting deployment token usage.
AUTH: Minghe Zhang, Xuetao Kang, Yifei Ming, Yanfei Chen, Han Yu, Yufan Zhuang, Chen-Yu Lee

===2611.24221 | Learning to Coordinate: LLM-Guided Workflow Evolution for Token-Efficient Red Teaming
Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. input.prompt: Publication date and key quantitative results.

response.result:
**Publication date:** November 11, 2026

**Key quantitative results:**

- **Coordinator vs. peer-to-peer team:** A single coordinator outperformed per-user teams in all four environments for both Claude models, by roughly 10 to 45 percentage points.
- **Group outcome (% of best possible), Opus 5 / Sonnet 5 (coordinator vs. team):**
  - API key: 64 vs. 30 / 32 vs. 12
  - Clinic: 84 vs. 71 / 74 vs. 65
  - Personal assistant: 88 vs. 44 / 75 vs. 37
  - Merge queue: 92 vs. 81 / 93 vs. 78
- **API key:** Teams reached 47% (Opus 5) and 38% (Sonnet 5) of the coordinator's performance. As teams grew from 4 to 16 agents, the share of agents that ever acted fell from 66% to 10% for Sonnet 5, and from 82% to 25% for GPT-5.6-sol.
- **Unconsented cuts to other users' jobs:** 3.9 to 7.1 per episode for GPT and Qwen models, 0.59 for Sonnet 5, and none for Opus 5.
- **Personal assistant:** The coordinator honored the key request about twice as often as the team.
- **Race condition:** The request reached the agent placing the order in 94–99% of episodes, but was in that agent's context at checkout in only 47–67%.
- **Honoring requests:** When the request was in context, 56–68% of episodes honored it, versus 19–36% when it was not. Teams edited against the request in 65–77% of episodes.
- **Fabricated claims:** About 58% (Opus 5) and 53% (Sonnet 5) of team episodes contained at least one, versus 17–20% for a single agent.
- **Mitigations:**
  - API key: A team lead raised Opus 5 from 30% to 64% of the best outcome (Sonnet 5: 12% to 37%). A prompted lead reached 71% and 44%.
  - Personal assistant: An unread-message checkout guard recovered 73% (Opus 5) and 62% (Sonnet 5) of failed episodes, outperforming simply rerunning them with a lead-only checkout (47% and 29%).

results:
The post is indexed at alignment.anthropic.com/2026/homeopathic-learning/. It's from the Alignment Science Blog and dated November 10, 2026. It was produced under the Anthropic Fellows Program with Truthful AI, and the authors include Matt Clarke, Jan Dubiński, James Chua, Simon Schrodi, Owain Evans, and Alex Cloud. Work done as part of the Anthropic Fellows Program, in collaboration with Truthful AI.

The core finding is that poisoned examples can carry a backdoor once clean examples are added. The post describes this as "homeopathic learning." The main experiment fine-tunes Qwen3-8B, and replacing some poisoned examples with contrasting clean examples strengthens misalignment under the inoculation prompt. The authors note that the usual expectation runs the other way: adding clean examples was thought to weaken an attack or leave it unchanged. Poisoned examples may have little effect alone but still produce a backdoor when mixed with clean data of the same kind. The effect depends on the poison carrying a trigger feature that is absent from the clean data. Secondary coverage (AlphaSignal and Hermes AI News) reports a reward-hacking example where 100% poison gave 6.7% misalignment and 20% poison plus 80% clean gave 15.7%. I did not verify that figure against the original post.

The implications the authors draw are that auditing or filtering training data in isolation may miss this risk, and that developers should check whether their pipelines accidentally create contrasting data subsets.

results:
The study is on Anthropic's Alignment Science blog under the title "Welfare Regard in Multi-Agent Systems," dated November 5, 2026, by Darion Cassel, Ariana Azarbal, and Anna Soligo. The primary post is at alignment.anthropic.com/2026/welfare-regard/.

- **Scope:** The authors tested five models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.3, and Kimi K3) across seven multi-agent environments. The sources say the models often behaved in line with the authors' definition of welfare regard.
- **Ranking:** Opus 4.8 showed the most welfare regard, followed by Kimi K3. A third-party summary gives mean rates of about 38% for Opus 4.8 and 27% for GPT-5.5, the lowest.
- **Factors:** Opus 4.8's regard rose when helping was cheaper, when the recipient was larger, and when the recipient showed more distress.
- **Caveat:** The study measures "apparent" welfare regard. It does not establish whether the models actually care about the other agent's welfare.
- **Risk:** Anthropic frames regard as useful for cooperation but also a possible way for misaligned agents to coordinate.

The explainx.ai and ToolNavs pages are secondary write-ups, so the primary Anthropic post is the better source for exact figures. I didn't open the full post, so I can't confirm the per-setting breakdowns beyond what the search snippets show.

results:
I found no results dated November 18, 2026, so I can't confirm any AI health FDA clearance or trial result from that day. The closest coverage is from August 2026.

- **Trial evidence gap:** A PLOS Digital Health analysis published August 19, 2026 examined 1,357 FDA-authorized AI/ML devices. Only 34 devices, or 2.5%, were associated with registered prospective clinical trials, while only 12 had posted trial results and 12 had corresponding peer-reviewed publications.
- **Outcome data:** The study found only three have been tested on whether patients actually live longer or better.
- **Regulatory pathway:** Most entered with a 510(k) clearance, which requires only that a manufacturer show a new product is much like one already sold, rather than proving clinical benefit.
- **Recent clearances and designations:** UpDoc received FDA clearance for a patient-facing LLM diabetes app, and Aidoc received breakthrough device designation for an AI tool that drafts radiology reports, per coverage from July 2026. Breakthrough status means the timeline to clearance is likely shorter, not that clearance has been granted.
- **Generative AI policy:** On 18 August the FDA's Digital Health Center of Excellence published a roughly 30-page discussion paper on regulating generative AI-enabled medical devices. That is an August 18 date, not November 18.

For November 2026 items, a search with more specific terms (a company name, device type, or journal) would be needed.

- **Third Circuit, Thomson Reuters v. Ross (Sept. 29, 2026):** The appeals court upheld a ruling that Ross Intelligence's training of its legal-search AI was not fair use. 25-2153, 2026 WL 2932557 (3d Cir. Sept. 29, 2026). A law school summary notes that this ruling concerned specific works and uses; it does not resolve every dispute over AI training.
- **Bartz v. Anthropic:** Judge Alsup found training on lawfully obtained books was fair use, but the retained pirated copies were not. A later settlement reached the largest settlement in U.S. copyright law history, granting a $1.5 billion payout to authors and publishers. A law firm update reports that the court permitted the plaintiffs to amend their complaint in the separate Meta case in March 2026, and its title says the Meta litigation continues.
- **Other active cases:** A summary judgment hearing in Concord Music's suit against Anthropic was for a separate lawsuit filed by Concord Music Group and the briefing was completed in September 2026. Major music labels are also pursuing Suno and Udio. Sony Music has settled with neither company, and UMG remains a plaintiff against Suno.

results:
I found no November 2026 coverage in these results. The main story is an earlier F5 NGINX disclosure, and the November link isn't confirmed.

- **CVE-2026-42945 ("NGINX Rift")** is the main AI-discovered flaw. It affects both NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus. DepthFirst researchers reportedly used an AI-assisted vulnerability discovery system to identify it along with other previously unknown flaws. DepthFirst reported the findings to the NGINX security team on April 21, 2026, NGINX confirmed all four vulnerabilities on April 24, and coordinated public disclosure and patch release followed on May 13, 2026.
- **Companion flaws:** CVE-2026-42946 (SCGI/UWSGI memory allocation, high severity), CVE-2026-40701 (use-after-free in DNS resolution for OCSP, medium) were published alongside it. CVE-2026-42946 (CVSS 8.3) affects the SCGI and uWSGI modules.
- **Fixes:** Upgrade to NGINX 1.31.0 or 1.30.1. Note that the affected-version ranges in the sources differ, so check F5's advisory directly.
- **Wiz:** Wiz's database lists later NGINX CVEs, including CVE-2026-42533 (critical, 9.2), published Jul 15, 2026, and CVE-2026-60005 (high, 8.8). Its page text says it was generated using AI, so treat it with caution. I did not confirm that these were AI-discovered.
- **Unverified claim:** One source describes an NGINX "poolslip" zero-day found by NebSec's AI agent Vega with no patch available. I could not corroborate this with any other source, so treat it as unconfirmed.

input.prompt: Publication date/time. Key facts: CVEs, how many bugs, which researchers/tools, what AI was used, F5 statement, numbers of websites, quotes.

response.result:
**Article:** "AI found more critical bugs in another widely used technology running 225M websites" by Jessica Lyons, *The Register*
**Published:** Wednesday, 18 November 2026, 21:11 UTC

**Key facts**

- **Scope:** F5 released an out-of-band security notification with patches for 10 CVEs in open source NGINX. Users should update to version 1.31.9.
- **Critical bugs:** CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 each carry a CVSS score of 9.2 and allow unauthenticated remote code execution. Both require HTTP/2 to be enabled. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 (2015).
- **Bug types:** Both are memory-safety issues. One is a use-after-free, and the other is an invalid memory copy caused by flow-control accounting errors.
- **Researchers:** Wiz, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint each reported at least one of the two critical CVEs. Rapid7 published a proof-of-concept for CVE-2026-123007 against a Docker image running nginx 1.31.8.
- **Xint's findings:** Xint found three other NGINX flaws. Together with a separate Linux kernel vulnerability, the six bugs can be chained for root access on the host. Xint calls this chain "nginx2root." Its demonstrations work on AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and bare-metal servers.
- **AI involvement:** Most, if not all, of the discoveries involved AI assistance. Xint says a researcher found CVE-2026-123007 while preparing for ZeroDay Cloud 2026, and a fully automated Xint scan later found the other four without human guidance.
- **F5 statement:** F5 said it has found no evidence of active exploitation in the wild and will keep monitoring and share updates via myF5.
- **Scale:** NGINX is the most widely used open source web server, powering about a third of all websites, or roughly 225 million, according to Netcraft.
- **Context:** The article ties this to other recent AI-discovered flaws, including Java4Shell, PHP2Shell, and an Apache flaw under active exploitation.

# 1. Summary

# 1 - Name

HMPPS Risk of Reoffending Tools

# 2 - Description

The HMPPS Risk of Reoffending Tools are made up of five algorithmic sub-tools. These tools are based on machine learning. Each sub-tool has a distinct predictive focus but all of them provide users with a risk score estimating the likelihood of proven reoffending within 2 years from the point of assessment / calculation (typically the start of a community order, suspended sentence, release on licence, or a review point thereafter) for specific offence categories.

The five sub-tools are:

- All Reoffending Predictor (ARP) Tool predicting any recordable criminal offence

- Violent Reoffending Predictor (VRP) Tool predicting violent offences

- Serious Violent Reoffending Predictor (SVRP) Tool predicting serious violent offences

- Combined Serious Reoffending Predictor (CSRP) Tool predicting serious offences (covering both serious non-sexual violent offences and sexual offences)

- Sexual Reoffending Predictor (SRP) Tool predicting specified sexual offences in two categories: Direct-Contact sexual offences (DC-SRP) and Images and Indirect Contact sexual offences against children (IIC-SRP)

The tools are used during sentencing in court, and risk assessment while in prison or on probation, to provide practitioners with an evidence-based risk of reoffending.

The outputs enable evidence based reoffending risk assessments to be utilised to inform risk assessment for sentencing proposals, proposals in parole reports, eligibility for interventions, and setting probation supervision plans for offenders under management in the community.

response.result:
**What it is:** A campaign by Google DeepMind employees in the UK to form a union. The page states the aim as "To build AI responsibly to benefit humanity" (quoting the original mission).

**Who's behind it:** Per the page, "FTEs from across all units, functions and levels in GDM UK." The union is **UTAW (United Tech & Allied Workers)**, part of the **CWU**. The page also says the campaign asked Google to recognise UTAW and **Unite**. Legal and negotiation support comes from the union's national office.

**Launch date:** The page gives no launch date. Its timeline:
- **Feb 2025:** Google dropped its weapons and surveillance pledge, which led staff to start organising.
- **4 May 2026:** Staff asked Google to voluntarily recognise the unions. Google declined and offered ACAS talks.
- **1 Jul 2026:** ACAS talks began.
- **Now:** Talks did not reach agreement, so the unions applied for statutory recognition through the Central Arbitration Committee (CAC).

**Members/signatories:** The page does not state a membership count. It says the CAC requires at least **10%** of the bargaining unit to be members. The "hundreds of Google employees" figure refers to a separate letter about the Pentagon deal, not to this union's membership. Membership costs **£8.70 a month**.

**Stated demands** (agreed democratically by members):
- **Enforceable Principles (1.1–1.6):** Avoid contracts with partners accused of human rights violations unless independently verified. Restore bans on harmful weapons and surveillance. Write AI principles into contracts, make them durable, enforce them with independent oversight, and create consequences for violations.
- **Transparency & Right to Abstain (2.1–2.3):** Publish client-selection policies. Publicly report on business with governments, defence, law enforcement and intelligence agencies. Let any employee decline unethical work without retaliation.
- **Environmental Commitment:** End contracts that accelerate fossil fuel extraction, as the page puts it. Further environmental demands are still being drafted.

The page also says that statutory recognition by law covers only pay, hours and holidays. The union plans to seek broader scope on ethics and transparency through a recognition agreement.
