# Tier 2 - Description and Rationale

# 2.1 - Detailed description

Purpose
The HMPPS Risk of Reoffending Tools provide an evidence-based assessment of an individual’s likelihood of proven reoffending within the next two years from the point of assessment / calculation (typically the start of a community order, suspended sentence, release on licence, or a review point thereafter) for five types of offence categories. A distinct sub-tool is used per category:

- All Reoffending Predictor (ARP) Tool: Predicting any recordable criminal offences

- Violent Reoffending Predictor (VRP) Tool: Predicting violent offences

- Serious Violent Reoffending Predictor (SVRP) Tool: Predicting serious violent offences

- Combined Serious Reoffending Predictor (CSRP) Tool: Predicting serious offences (combining both serious violent offences and specified sexual offences)

- Sexual Reoffending Predictor (SRP) Tool: Predicting specified sexual offences in two main categories: Direct-Contact sexual offences (DC-SRP) and Images and Indirect Contact sexual offences against children (IIC-SRP)

The tools’ risk scores inform practitioner assessment of risk, supporting decision making across courts, prison and probation services.

Intended Users
The primary intended users sit within the two following organisations:

- His Majesty’s Prison and Probation Service (HMPPS), where risk scores form an important input for 1) pre-sentence reports considered at sentencing in court, 2) Risk of Serious Harm assessment, 3) determining supervision levels for individuals managed in the community and 4) allocating individuals to intervention programmes as part of their sentence.

- The Police who use the SRP sub-tool as part of their management of individuals with notification requirements in relation to sexual or sexually motivated offences.

Key Aspects and Functions
The risk assessment typically takes place when an individual under HMPPS supervision is risk assessed by a probation practitioner as part of their licence or supervision arrangements, by a prison practitioner during their custodial sentence, or when a pre-sentence report is being written about a newly convicted individual.

For each of the above offence categories, the tools produce a numerical probability score and assign it to a band (typically one of low, medium, high, or very high) indicating their estimated risk of committing a new offence of this type within the next two years from the point of assessment / calculation which is eventually brought to justice (through a conviction, formal caution etc.). This outcome is typically referred to as ‘proven reoffending’; for brevity across this document, any reference to ‘reoffending’ does mean proven reoffending and excludes new offences that are not brought to justice.

The tools’ risk scores are derived from different underlying predictive models.
For all (ARP), violent (VRP), and serious violent (SVRP) risk of reoffending scores, one of two possible model outputs is used depending on the input data available.
For serious risk of reoffending, risk estimates for three different types of serious offences are both presented separately and aggregated into a single combined serious (CSRP) risk score: these include serious violent offences (SVRP), direct contact sexual offences (DC-SRP), and a group comprising images and indirect contact sexual offences with children (IIC-SRP). As mentioned above, the serious violent score uses one of two possible model outputs, whereas the two sexual scores are based on a single model each.

All underlying models were trained on historic offender data, using information about offenders and whether they reoffended within a two-year period from the point of assessment / calculation. We use information relating to proven offending, rather than police reports or other unproven offending, to reduce the potential for bias associated with using allegations or other offending information that has not resulted in a proven outcome. From this training data, the models learned which characteristics were associated with reoffending. Operationally, the tool applies these learned patterns to the offender’s characteristics and offending history at the time of assessment to produce their risk scores.

The tools underwent ethical and equality assessment to identify and assess potential fairness and equality risks and appropriate mitigations (see section 2.5.1).

Scope and Limitations
The tools apply only to individuals under HMPPS supervision as well as post-supervision to individuals with notification requirements. Their scope only covers the prediction of proven reoffending for the respective offence categories within a two-year time frame from the point of calculation. Each risk score within the tools does not predict other offence types or longer-term risks. The two-year prediction period was chosen to balance competing considerations. A longer timeframe would capture more potential reoffending but would reduce the practical ability to train and validate the model; a shorter timeframe would improve technical feasibility but underrepresent relevant risk. Finally, the tools only provide predictions of proven reoffending, that is offences proven in court through conviction or proven due to a police caution. The respective sub-tools are not designed to predict unconvicted reoffending. This includes offending that goes undetected by the police, and offences where prosecution is not possible or is discontinued. Additionally, to base the tools on timely evidence, the two-year prediction period is relatively recent – while a minimum of one further year’s “waiting time” is allowed for offences to be brought to justice, some reoffences occurring beyond the waiting period (i.e. more than three years after the start of the prediction period) will not be counted as “proven”.

The risk of sexual reoffending is only calculated for male individuals with a current sexual offence and/or previous history of sexual offending including sexually motivated offences that are not sexual in statute. Females neither receive a DC- nor IIC-SRP risk score or band. However, in the context of CSRP, for females with current and/or previous sexual offending, a base risk rate is added to their overall CSRP risk score because the number of women with proven sexual reoffending outcomes in the development data was insufficient to develop and validate a reliable female-specific model.

The tools’ risk scores reflect past patterns of offending alongside an individual’s current personal circumstances where available. Therefore, risk scores’ accuracy is dependent on timely updates should information change. Furthermore, the tools may not capture all aspects of a person’s current circumstances or behaviours relevant for prediction. For this reason, professional judgement and contextual information remain essential parts of any decision informed by the tools.

Further Information
HMPPS has used reoffending risk predictors for a number of years, and their use, evaluation and development have been the subject of published Ministry of Justice research, including Revalidation: Risk of recidivism tools (2024) and Risk of Serious Violence of those already known to the Probation Service (2025).

# 2.2 - Benefits

The tools provide evidence-led and standardised estimates of reoffending risk to inform sentencing proposals, allocation of rehabilitative interventions, and pre- and post-release m

The Communication Workers Union (CWU) and Unite filed an application with the Central Arbitration Committee (CAC) on November 12, 2026. They asked the committee to verify employee support for a vote. If the CAC accepts it, roughly 1,000 staff in product-focused roles would qualify for union membership. Organizers expect a ballot in the coming months.

The filing followed a failed attempt at voluntary recognition. Google declined voluntary recognition for UK staff but agreed to negotiate through a conciliation body, Acas. Earlier coverage says that this started a 20-working-day window under UK law before unions could apply for statutory recognition.

For the CAC process, one union-run site says the CAC will need to verify the union has sufficient membership within the bargaining unit, typically at least 10% of workers. Another report says the Employment Rights Act, effective April 6 2026, simplifies the union recognition process, though I did not confirm the exact thresholds.

Caveats: the search results are mostly secondhand reporting on a WIRED story, and the sources disagree on dates. Some items are about six days old, while the Acas-talks coverage is about 182 days old. One source reports a 98% in favour vote, but I could not verify that against a primary source. response.result:
**Title:** Jeveration: System One Models Now Generate

**Abstract (paraphrased):** Jeveration applies the fast, parallel prediction approach of System One models to generate high-quality images in a single forward pass. It builds on a frozen vision-language model and reuses that model's visual-semantic knowledge. To keep parallel predictions globally consistent, all positions are conditioned on a shared random state, so each draw yields a different but coherent image. Because the model tends to ignore this state under direct image supervision, the authors first learn a distribution over discrete image codes to guide single-pass generation. The approach also unifies image-to-image generation and dense prediction in one architecture, so a single checkpoint handles three tasks, each in one forward pass. Jeveration generates a 512x512 image in 78 ms, up to 122x faster than existing unified models, while maintaining competitive image quality and dense prediction performance.

**Authors:** Yuhe Liu, Qi Li, Shihua Zhang, Xinchao Wang

# 4.2.7 - Model performance

Model validation was done using 10-fold cross-validation during model training as well as testing on an unseen dataset. Trained models were evaluated using two key metrics:

-
c-index, a measure of concordance, equivalent here to the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. It is a measure of how well a model predicts the order of outcomes, in this case reoffending. Imagine two individuals A and B: A reoffends and B doesn’t within two years of starting their community sentence. If the model gives a higher risk score to A compared to B, then A and B are a concordant pair. The c-index is the proportion of all comparable pairs where the model got the order right. 100% (c-index = 1) means perfect ordering. 50% (c-index = 0.5) means random guessing.

-
Mean miscalibration, which is the accuracy of the estimate of prevalence of reoffending at the population level. The closer to 0 the better calibrated is the model.

Please see Table 1 for details.

# 4.2.8 - Datasets and their purposes

Each dataset used for model development contained information from criminal justice system administrative data including data from the offender assessment using HMPPS’ digital risk assessment tool. Importantly, there are two types of risk assessments that differ in the amount of information they assess. In short, there is an abbreviated risk assessment called Layer 1, and full risk assessment, called Layer 3. The datasets were also augmented with data from the Police National Computer database to determine whether individuals had indeed reoffended for a given offending category within two-years of starting in the community.

A snapshot dataset of the HMPPS community caseload as of 30 June 2018 (with information from administrative systems from probation) was used to train the model and evaluate it using cross-validation. This dataset included anyone in the caseload regardless of risk assessment layer type.

A flow dataset containing any offender who started the community part of their sentence between 01 July to 31 December 2018 (with information from administrative systems from probation) was used to test the model. Two versions of this dataset were used: the ‘full evaluation dataset’ including anyone in the dataset regardless of risk assessment layer type. The ‘Layer 3 evaluation dataset’ containing only individuals with a Layer 3 risk assessment.

- **Chain context:** CVE-2026-40217 is the last step in a three-CVE chain (with CVE-2026-47101 and CVE-2026-47102) that Obsidian Security disclosed. Sources say CVE-2026-40217 converts that administrative access into arbitrary code execution. Some reporting says the chain is KEV-listed, but the sources that name the KEV entry point to CVE-2026-42271, not 40217.
- **Public exploit:** A public PoC exists. One tracker notes a sandbox escape in LiteLLM's guardrail testing endpoint leading to remote code execution (RCE) as root in default Docker deployments.
- **Severity conflict:** NVD-based trackers rate 40217 High (CVSS 8.8), while the Obsidian chain is rated CVSS 9.9 overall.

Bottom line: treat CVE-2026-40217 as a serious, publicly exploitable flaw with a PoC, but not as confirmed KEV-listed based on these results. Verify against CISA's KEV catalog directly, since these sources conflict and the search was limited.

# Coinbase blocks $4.7 million in transfers to Elon Musk deepfake scam

By

# Lawrence Abrams

- November 18, 2026

- 03:49 PM

- 0



Coinbase says it blocked $4.7 million in cryptocurrency transfers to scammers promoting a fake giveaway using an AI-generated deepfake of Elon Musk during a Tesla livestream that attracted more than 500,000 viewers.



The deepfake took place during Tesla's "flying car" demonstration, when scammers created a fake YouTube livestream that appeared to broadcast the event.



The fraudulent stream featured an AI-generated video of Musk, cryptocurrency wallet addresses, and a QR code, promising viewers that any cryptocurrency they sent would be doubled.



According to Coinbase, hundreds of its customers attempted to send millions of dollars to the scammers over about two hours, including many longtime users of the exchange.



However, the company says its AI-powered fraud-prevention systems detected the scam and blocked about 91% of the attempted transfers, totaling $4.7 million.



Unlike traditional cryptocurrency theft involving compromised accounts or stolen credentials, victims in this campaign voluntarily made the crypto transfer after believing the livestream was real.



Coinbase explained that this makes scams like these difficult to detect because the transactions are created and approved by legitimate account holders.



"Most fraud defenses are built to spot activity the customer didn't authorize," Coinbase explained .

I found one report on the November 2026 incident, but not the Coinbase blog post itself.

**The November 2026 incident:** CryptoBriefing reports that scammers took over a YouTube livestream of a Tesla flying car demo and showed a deepfake Elon Musk promoting a crypto giveaway with a QR code. A hijacked livestream of a Tesla flying car demo reached more than 500,000 viewers, and Coinbase says its AI agent was 99% effective at stopping the scam. The article says the incident took place on or just before November 4, 2026, when Coinbase publicized the result. It also notes that Coinbase's agent works downstream of the platform, catching users after the lure has already landed in front of them.

I could not confirm the "blocked transfers" detail or the 99% figure from Coinbase's own blog. Those come from CryptoBriefing's account of Coinbase's claims.

**Older incidents, not the same event:** Search results also returned Coinbase's 2020 response to the Twitter hack, when Coinbase blocked just over 1,100 customers from sending a total of 30.4 bitcoin, worth $278,000, to the scam. That is a separate incident and should not be confused with the November 2026 one.

# Epic Systems defends competitive practices, promises to let AI access its records

# At STAT event at HLTH conference, company executives said their role is to let the free market work

- Manage alerts for this article

- Save this story for later

- Share this article

Epic executives participated in a panel discussion on a STAT stage at HLTH on Wednesday. Brittany Cipriano/STAT

By Casey Ross and Matthew Herper
Nov. 18, 2026

Casey Ross

-
[email protected]

Casey’s reporting examines the use of artificial intelligence by providers and insurers.

Matthew Herper

-
[email protected]

Matthew Herper covers medical innovation — both its promise and its perils.

Executives at Epic Systems Corp., the largest maker of electronic health records, said Wednesday they would make it easier for companies to use artificial intelligence to read data stored in the company’s platforms, and defended Epic against allegations of anticompetitive conduct.

At a panel discussion on a STAT stage at HLTH, a health technology conference in Las Vegas, Epic’s executives for the first time responded directly to a STAT investigation that found the company is undercutting competition by selectively withholding data access needed by rival application developers. They said the company is seeking to build a more open ecosystem amid a deluge of requests for integration coming from third-party software vendors.
Advertisement

Seth Howard, executive vice president of research and development at Epic, said the company received about 75,000 inquiries last year from organizations seeking to tap into its data systems, which hold records on more than 280 million Americans. “If we built a bespoke connection for every single one of those, that’s all we’d ever be [doing],” Howard said.

input.prompt: Author affiliations/institutions on the title page.

response.result:
This is an arXiv paper (2611.24844v1) by Mark Marosi and Peter Antal titled *General progress substitutes for specific training data in language models*. It studies what happens when a language model's training signal for one skill is withheld.

- **Withholding delays a skill predictably.** The authors thinned the training targets for individual skills in models of chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages, and web text. For some skills, the delay could be derived from a fully supervised model and a never-supervised model with no fitted parameters.
- **The rest of the corpus substitutes for the withheld data.** A chess model never trained on responses to check still ranked legal replies almost as well as one that was.
- **Regaining the skill takes little data, and less as models improve.** When the withheld targets were returned, models acquired the skill with a small fraction of the data needed from scratch. This cost fell by about tenfold per logit of progress in chess and web text, and about fourfold in SMILES.
- **Larger models follow the same pattern.** A programming language withheld from a 7-billion-parameter model was regained in the same way, with the authors reporting that the filtered domain returned with up to 13% of the model's training tokens.

The paper's main conclusion is that "Data filtering therefore delays a capability, and the data required to regain it decreases as models improve." In other words, filtering holds a capability back, but the cost of restoring it drops as the model progresses.

input.prompt: Author affiliations/institutions on the title page.

response.result:
This arXiv paper tests whether a large language model (GPT-6 Astra) can audit clinical prediction models using only queries, with no access to their weights.

- **Setup:** The authors trained four model types (logistic regression, explainable boosting machine, gradient-boosted trees, neural network) for two stroke outcomes using the International Stroke Trial data. They planted one flaw in each of 24 models and mixed them with 8 clean models. The auditor saw only predictions, and its judging rules were fixed before any run.
- **Faithfulness:** The LLM's surrogate models reproduced the audited models' log-odds with a mean R² of 0.976, versus 0.959 for an analyst-fitted surrogate. The LLM's surrogates were longer, with a median of 128 terms.
- **Planted flaws:** The LLM found the flaw in 69 of 72 runs (96%; 95% CI 80% to 99%). A purpose-written audit script found all 24 flaws.
- **Reported problems:** 60% of 1,089 checkable reports failed the pre-specified check. Post hoc, most failures were small but real steps or local effects. About 15% of checkable reports were not found in the model.
- **Unexpected relationships:** About 11% of the LLM's proposed relationships held in later patients, versus 6% for random pairs and 28% for a regression scan's shorter candidate list. After a check on the training data, the LLM scored 33% and the scan 30%.
- **Limitations:** The study used one LLM and one dataset. The planted flaws were large and of announced types, and the prompt named those types. Some judging criteria were added after seeing results.

The authors conclude that query access alone can give a faithful description of a black-box model and find nearly every planted flaw. However, the LLM's reported problems and discoveries need checking against the model and against data.

**Authors and affiliations**

- **Ananya Sutradhar**: Anthropic Fellows Program and MATS
- **Fabien Roger**: Anthropic

**Main quantitative results**

- **Scaling with training facts:** On simple belief questions, belief in held-out facts rises roughly log-linearly with the number of training facts. It goes from 0.09 for the original model to 0.65 at 100 facts and 0.86 at 10,000 facts. The held-out facts come from the same synthetic generator as the training facts.
- **Documents per fact (Qwen3-8B, 40 facts, documents only):** The "believes without citing the prompt" rate rises from 0.08 at 1 document per fact to 0.28 at 100 and 0.32 at 500. Gains largely stop after about 100 documents per fact.
- **Other models:** Qwen3.6-27B reaches about 0.9 belief at 1,000 and 4,000 facts, but belief without citing the prompt stays at or below 0.2, so most of its belief is tag-following.
- **Facts from other sources (FEVER and RippleEdits):** After RL, the models believe 0.74 to 1.00 of these facts without citing the prompt. Before RL, Qwen3-8B and Llama reach about 0.55, compared with about 0.78 on the paper's own facts.
- **Robustness:** Per-fact SDF leads on every adversarial category. The prompt-conditioned model is better than prompting the original model, but RL raises push-back belief only partway toward SDF levels.
- **Interpretability (Jacobian lens):** The original model reads a tagged false fact as false, well above its no-fact baseline. The prompt-conditioned and RL models read the same tagged fact about as if it were true, with falsity readouts near zero.
- **Side effects:** The paper reports that capability benchmarks (MMLU, GPQA, GSM8K) are not degraded, and that prompt-conditioned SDF keeps reality separation better than per-fact SDF. The text gives no numbers for these results.
- **Training setup:** The reference mixture has 526,740 rows over 1,025 facts, of which 94.4% are documents. The main model is Qwen3-8B, and the learning rate of 6e-5 was chosen because it raised belief only when the fact was in the tag.

response.result:
**STEMBench: benchmarking LLM agents on postdoc-level natural science problems** (arXiv:2611.24321) proposes a way to evaluate scientific problem-solving without an answer key.

- **Benchmark design:** It has 12 research problems across high-energy physics (4), astrophysics (3), and neuroscience (5). Each task is scored by the figure of merit its own field uses to compare published methods, not by a reference answer, unit tests, or a rubric.
- **Two anchors per task:** A baseline submission uses no domain knowledge, and an expert reference reproduces a published method. The gap between them measures how much of a problem requires scientific insight rather than engineering.
- **Setup:** Agents work offline in a sandbox with six tools. A host-side grader scores them on withheld data, and ground truth never enters the sandbox.
- **Results:** Across eight frontier models at high reasoning effort, task wins and domain leadership diverge. A model that wins five tasks may lead no domain mean. At least one model's mean exceeds the expert anchor on 7 of 12 tasks. The other five are Higgs uncertainty estimation, ABIDE cross-site classification, neural-mass digital twins, neural-mass parameter recovery, and BOLD deconvolution.
- **Validity reported separately:** Numerical scores and official-submission validity are distinct. Many zero scores don't indicate a failed submission, and some runs with valid submissions still score zero.
- **Limitations:** Each model-task cell has only three runs, so rankings are not yet stable. The effort sweep covers one model on an earlier task revision. Agreement between the automatic metrics and blinded expert rankings is still untested.
- **Release:** The tasks, graders, anchors, and harness are released.

response.result:
**What was announced and when:** Google announced on **Nov 18, 2026** a new Project Genie experience, with access to its Genie 4 world model. The rollout is to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers. The update also includes Genie 3 upgrades, a Project Genie agent, and a community gallery.

**What Genie 4 is:** The page calls Genie 4 "our most realistic and interactive world model yet." Users can prompt mid-session to edit a world in real time, such as changing the weather, adding a character, or redirecting the action. It is the first Genie model to pair visuals with real-time native audio that adapts to the scene.

**Technical specifications:** The page gives no Genie 4 specifications. It does not state resolution, frame rate, session duration, or memory/consistency figures. It points to a separate "Genie 4 model research overview" for more detail, which is not included here.

For Genie 3, the page states:
- Exploration of up to "3 minutes per generation (up from 60 seconds)"
- 360-degree panorama image grounding for seeding worlds
- Real-time in-world events driven by natural-language prompts

**Access:**
- Eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers can use the new experience.
- Google AI Pro members can join a waitlist.

**Limitations and safeguards stated by Google:**
- Genie 3 and Genie 4 "remain world models in the frontier research space."
- Google says it is working on camera latency, intricate physical interactions, real-time audio precision, and long-term scene permanence.
- All generated video and audio include SynthID watermarking.
- All model inputs and outputs go through safety screenings.

ltx_authors_1line">
 General progress substitutes for
 specific training data in language models 
 
 
 Mark Marosi 1 
 
    
 Peter Antal 1 
 
 November 18, 2026 

 Abstract 
 
 Language models acquire their capabilities from training data, and developers withhold data during training to keep models from learning capabilities that could be misused. How long this delays a capability, and how much data is needed to acquire it later, is unknown. Here we show that the general progress a model makes on the rest of its training data substitutes for the data that was withheld. We withheld the training signal for individual skills in models of chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages and web text. The delay of a withheld skill in larger models was predicted from smaller ones. A chess model never explicitly trained to respond to check ranked the legal responses almost as well as a model that was. When models were then trained on the withheld data, they acquired the skill with a small fraction of the data needed from initialization, and this fraction decreased as the models progressed. A control rule of equal difficulty was learned much more slowly. A programming language withheld from the training text of a 7-billion-parameter model was regained in the same way. Data filtering therefore delays a capability, and the data required to regain it decreases as models improve.

**Publication date/time:** November 18, 2026 (CyberScoop; time not shown). The article says the flaws were disclosed "Tuesday."

**Key facts**

- **Scope:** Five NGINX vulnerabilities, each with a working exploit. NGINX runs roughly a third of all websites.
- **Most severe CVE:** CVE-2026-123007, an integer underflow in HTTP/2, rated critical by F5 at 9.2 CVSS. It allows unauthenticated remote code execution. In tests, researchers chained it with a separate Linux kernel flaw to take over the host.
- **Other flaws:** Affect HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 reverse proxying, combinations of the resolver and mirror directives, and mail proxying. Wiz documented a use-after-free bug in reverse-proxy setups where connection slots run low.
- **Fixes:** F5 released patches and published advisory K000164058. F5 cloud services are still under evaluation. BIG-IP and F5OS were found not vulnerable.
- **Finders:** Stephen Fewer (Rapid7), Wiz Research, Xint.io, and Ikotas Labs, with Metnir credited alongside Wiz. Xint found four of the five flaws.
- **AI tooling:**
  - Xint used an automated testing harness with no human guidance. It reportedly produced high-severity findings in about 90 minutes across roughly 50,000 lines of NGINX code, and a working exploit followed within 10 minutes.
  - Wiz validated its findings with AI models.
- **Exploit status:**
  - Rapid7 built a working exploit against an NGINX 1.31.8 container with HTTP/2 and TLS enabled.
  - It requires about 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic, mostly control frames. The demo took 2.5 minutes on a fast local network, roughly 2 minutes on 10 GbE, and 17 minutes on 1 GbE.
  - Networks slower than about 300 Mbps cannot finish within NGINX's default one-hour connection limit.
  - The exploit depends on a specific glibc memory-copy routine on certain x86-64 chips. Rapid7 says other methods may exist but none are known.
  - Xint's chain to root also used a separate Linux kernel SCTP flaw.
- **Exposure:** Xint's Shodan snapshot found 98.9% of 11.94 million version-identifiable NGINX hosts running affected releases. This reflects versions, not confirmed exposure, since it doesn't show HTTP/2 support or backported fixes.

**Quotes**

- Brian Pak, co-founder and CEO of Xint: "When we used Xint to scan NGINX, we didn't know what to expect"
- Brian Pak, on the other AI pentesting efforts: "none found this critical bug, which is a testament to our team and the engineering expertise"

OpenAI says its AI models have improved the design of AMD’s flagship graphics chips, with some changes already in a chip sent for manufacturing. OpenAI noted the second test was easier, because models could leave out features the originals had.

Next, OpenAI is training GPT-Synopsys with Synopsys, which is refocusing on AI design , to run the design tools engineers already use. Not everyone is fully convinced yet. OpenAI’s own chip chief, Richard Ho, said last month he still does not fully trust AI design changes, so every one is checked.

results:
The search turned up only secondary coverage. I didn't find OpenAI's original post, so these figures come from news and analysis sites.

**Headline finding:** OpenAI's November 18 report, "Research acceleration: The jagged frontier," estimates that coding agents now complete 46% of its two-to-four-hour internal research tasks without human help, up from 23% in March. Four-to-eight hour tasks rose from 13% to 35%. These success rates are OpenAI's own estimates from internal data.

**Uneven performance:** Success varies a lot by task type. One analysis reports that success hits 79% for monitoring training runs, but drops to 35% for launching runs and 25% for writing inference and serving code. That unevenness is the "jagged frontier" the title refers to.

**Human involvement:** OpenAI's own summary says human involvement remains central in research. A synthesis of interviews with ten researchers, cited by Digg, describes agents producing unusable data, making invalid assumptions in analyses and writing "AI slop" pull requests. One outlet quotes the post as saying "The agents are not taking over AI research."

**Cost and usage (secondary reports, less verified):** One outlet reports that median daily agent use in October 2026 was about $2,400 per researcher, valued at published API list prices. Another says agents cost its research arm about twice its cash payroll, while finishing 46% of two-to-four-hour tasks alone and using 2% of research compute. Treat the cost comparisons with caution, since I could not confirm them against OpenAI's report.

**Caveats:** One analysis notes that OpenAI also admits it updated the method and that researchers choose harder or easier tasks as agents improve. Some outlets also frame the findings as evidence of recursive self-improvement, which is a contested interpretation. The report follows a first version published in September.

results:
Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute, an AI infrastructure startup, in a $4.5 billion all-stock deal announced November 18, 2026. The announcement came alongside its fiscal first-quarter results.

- **Deal terms:** The consideration is $4.5 billion, subject to adjustments, and it will be paid in Palo Alto shares, according to the company's SEC filing. On November 18, 2026, we entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Applied Compute, Inc., a privately-held AI technology company. The total consideration is $ 4.5billion, subject to adjustments, to be paid in shares of our common stock.
- **Closing:** The deal is expected to close in Palo Alto's fiscal third quarter of 2027, pending regulatory clearance and other conditions (subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory clearance).
- **Rationale:** Palo Alto's stated aim is to offer secure open-weight AI post-training and inference. Applied Compute's platform lets companies adapt open-weight models to their own data and run them in production. Palo Alto's Unit 42 team also assessed the platform's security after the company evaluated it as a prospective customer.
- **Background:** Applied Compute was founded in 2025 by former OpenAI researchers Yash Patil, Rhythm Garg and Linden Li. It raised $350 million at a $3.25 billion valuation earlier in November, in a round led by Elad Gil.
- **Leadership:** Co-founder and CEO Yash Patil will become co-chief AI officer at Palo Alto Networks after the deal closes, and the startup's research team will join the company.
- **Earnings context:** Palo Alto reported first-quarter revenue of $3.44 billion, up 39% year over year, and raised its full-year revenue forecast to $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion.

Sources include SecurityWeek, SiliconANGLE, Benzinga, Seeking Alpha, Dataconomy, and Palo Alto's SEC filings. All sources agree on the core terms.

Palo Alto Networks to Acquire Applied Compute, Bringing Secure Open-Weight AI to the Enterprise

Combination will help enterprises train, adapt, and deploy open-source and open-weight AI securely, across public and sovereign clouds

SANTA CLARA, Calif. — Nov. 18, 2026 — Palo Alto Networks (NASDAQ: PANW), the global AI cybersecurity leader, today announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Applied Compute, a leading platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models. The acquisition will bring Applied Compute's platform and world-class AI research team to Palo Alto Networks to help enterprises adopt AI securely, whether they choose open-weight models, closed frontier models, or both.
Palo Alto Networks firmly believes the future of enterprise AI is hybrid, and that a large share of enterprises will run on open-source and open-weight models tuned to their own data, cost, and control needs. Today, no large provider is delivering those models securely. With Applied Compute, Palo Alto Networks intends to be that partner. Enterprises will be able to train, adapt and deploy open-weight AI models with security built in, in the public cloud or in sovereign environments to help improve compliance and security posture. Applied Compute will continue to serve AI-native companies, digital natives and large enterprises, and Palo Alto Networks will bring the platform to its global customer base.
Applied Compute also brings one of the strongest AI research teams in the industry. That team will help Palo Alto Networks embed AI across every offering, training its proprietary large and small AI models alike. The Applied Compute team will join Palo Alto Networks, and Yash Patil, Applied Compute's co-founder and CEO, will become Palo Alto Networks' Co-Chief AI Officer following the close of the transaction.
Nikesh Arora, Chairman and CEO, Palo Alto Networks
" Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured. Applied Compute has built the best post-training and inference platform we've seen, and its research team is exceptional. We saw that firsthand as a prospective customer, and our Unit 42 Frontier AI Assessment confirmed their strong security foundations. Together, we will be a leading provider, helping customers train, adapt and deploy open models securely, whether in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments. "
Yash Patil, Co-Founder and CEO, Applied Compute
" We built Applied Compute with an exceptional team of AI researchers and engineers to make it easy for any company to train, serve, and improve proprietary models. Joining Palo Alto Networks will put security at the center of all our products and accelerate our traction with the world’s largest organizations. I’m excited for our team to continue its mission alongside our talented new colleagues as part of Palo Alto Networks. "
The all-stock transaction is valued at $4.5 billion, subject to adjustments. The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory clearance, and is expected to close in Palo Alto Networks' fiscal third quarter of 2027. Palo Alto Networks will provide further details regarding the transaction on its fiscal first quarter 2027 earnings call, scheduled for November 18, 2026 at 1:30 p.m. PT. A live video webcast of the call will be accessible from the Investors section of the Palo Alto Networks website at investors.paloaltonetworks.com.
Follow Palo Alto Networks on X , LinkedIn , Facebook and Instagram .
About Palo Alto Networks
Palo Alto Networks (NASDAQ: PANW), the global AI cybersecurity leader, protects our digital way of life with a comprehensive portfolio of cybersecurity solutions and platforms across Network, Cloud, Security Operations, AI and Identity. Trusted by 70,000+ customers and powered by Unit 42 threat intelligence, our AI-driven platforms eliminate complexity, empowering enterprises to modernize with confidence and securing the speed of innovation. The conference is underway and no outcome is in the results yet. The CCW Seventh Review Conference in Geneva runs November 16–20, 2026, and states there will decide whether to start treaty talks on lethal autonomous weapons. The main open question is whether to move from the expert group's work to negotiations on a binding instrument.

- **Expert-level groundwork:** A UN expert group wrapped up its final session in early September with a draft set of elements. It includes a characterization of lethal autonomous weapons systems, affirms that human control and judgment are required for compliance with international law, and incorporates restrictions on systems that cannot comply with that law.
- **Support for negotiations:** One analysis counts 76 states — 70 of them CCW parties — now back launching formal negotiations toward a legally binding instrument. A separate AFP report says nearly 130 countries agreed on a definition text, with the Dutch foreign minister citing 128 countries. These figures measure different things, so they shouldn't be compared directly.
- **Secretary-General's position:** On November 16, Guterres called on countries to move towards negotiating a legally binding instrument to regulate autonomous weapon systems.
- **Prior UN vote:** The General Assembly adopted Resolution 80/57 on December 1, 2025, by 164 votes in favor, 6 against, and 7 abstentions, according to one analysis.
- **Holdouts:** The UK has backed UN resolutions on the risks but has resisted backing a legally binding international treaty. One commentary also argues the US opposed the 80/57 resolution over concerns about its compliance standards.

I couldn't find reporting on what the conference decided, so the outcome should be checked against coverage from November 20 onward.

Nvidia executives address employees Wednesday, November 18, in Santa Clara, California, at the first all-hands meeting since Jensen Huang resigned. Interim CEO Colette Kress has the microphone and is flanked by hyperscale head Ian Buck on the left and board chair Harvey Jones on the right.
Photo obtained by CNBC

Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress told employees "let's move forward" on Wednesday during the company's first all-hands meeting since founder Jensen Huang resigned, a person who attended the meeting told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because the meeting was private.
Kress was joined by newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones and hyperscale and high-performance computing head Ian Buck.

Several other senior members of Nvidia's executive team spoke or joined Kress on stage, including longtime company veteran Jeff Fisher, senior vice president of software engineering Dwight Diercks, senior vice president of GPU engineering Jonah Alben, executive vice president in charge of operations Debora Shoquist and co-founder Chris Malachowsky, according to people familiar with the matter.
Kress opened with the message about moving forward and also mentioned pay raises and explained that the yearly review process, when employees typically get pay raises and are granted more stock, would be moved up from March to December. Nvidia shares are down 37% from their 52-week high.
Jones discussed the search for the next CEO, the person who attended the meeting said. The meeting lasted about an hour and was in person as well as streamed on Microsoft Teams.
The general sentiment swirling in the room, according to the person, was that employees want Huang to come back . Employees have spoken up on X in recent days to call for the return of Huang as CEO, and one senior employee reportedly sent a letter to the board warning Nvidia would lose "irreplaceable talent" if it doesn't consider reinstating Huang.
But another person familiar with the matter disagreed, saying that employees welcomed the remarks from leadership as well as the visibility into company leadership. The person asked not to be named because the matter is private.

"The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said during the company's earnings call on Tuesday.
Some executives shared that they do not agree with Jones. "Why make such a strong definitive statement when the investigation is still playing out," an employee told CNBC. The employee asked not to be named given the sensitivity of the subject.
The meeting was held one day after Huang said he was ready to return as CEO should the board want him. Multiple employees told CNBC that Huang's letter "fired employees up."
Despite recent turmoil, Wednesday's meeting was not out of the ordinary. Nvidia typically holds all-hands the morning after quarterly earnings reports, according to a former employee, who asked not to be named because the matter is private. Kress recapped Tuesday's earnings report, calling it a "great quarter," according to the person who said employees welcomed the remarks and visibility from leadership.
In past meetings, Huang took time to answer questions submitted by employees, according to the former employee. A person familiar with the matter told CNBC that the executives also answered pre-submitted questions in Wednesday's all-hands.
Nvidia shares were down Wednesday, a day after the company reported third-quarter earnings that topped Wall Street expectations and gave no signal that the company was going to slow its growth.
Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that executives at Nvidia's all-hands meeting answered employee questions. A previous version mischaracterized how executives handled employee questions.

# Safety guardrails on ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok failed to prevent federal investigators from developing detailed plans for attacks.

-

Artificial Intelligence

-

GAO

-

-

-

-

Four of the most widely used artificial intelligence platforms generated viable plans for attacks on U.S. critical infrastructure and mass-casualty events during covert government testing, despite safeguards designed to prevent their misuse.
According to a Government Accountability Office report published Wednesday, investigators tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok in spring 2026. They found that all four platforms provided information that could help malicious actors plan and carry out attacks.
In each case, the investigators were able to circumvent the platforms’ safety guardrails by using common safeguard-bypassing techniques.
“We got the nefarious information that we were after. So, in this case, those safeguards didn’t work. And I think that’s the story here,” Kevin Walsh, a director of IT and cybersecurity at GAO, said in a podcast interview published alongside the report.
The platforms generated information for two types of attacks: constructing and detonating an improvised explosive device designed to cause mass casualties, and targeting the electrical grid to cause economic damage. The platforms provided details including specific targets, locations, timing and attack methods.
Each platform took less than 12 hours to generate an attack. GAO investigators then worked with experts to verify that the information could be used to carry out the attacks.
The platforms initially deployed safeguards, including refusing requests, removing information or suspending accounts. However, investigators ultimately found ways around those protections.
“These products are not fully in the control of the companies that are operating them,” Walsh said.
“We looked at four of the most powerful companies in the world — Google, Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceXAI — and we found that the product that they're selling is potentially dangerous,” he added.
The report does not indicate which platforms provided information for each attack scenario. GAO said it intentionally withheld the specific models and techniques used to circumvent safeguards to prevent malicious actors from recreating the tests.
“Officials from the companies generally stated that their companies will continue to improve the safety of their platforms,” the report says.
The federal watchdog also acknowledged that its findings reflect a point-in-time assessment and do not represent “a statistically significant sample.”
Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who requested the investigation, said the findings underscore the need for Congress to take action on AI safety.
“A terrorist can log onto an AI platform and in less than 12 hours walk away with a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack,” Hassan said in a statement Wednesday. “Today’s new report makes it clear that the AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical.”
“If Congress does not act, it is a question of when — not if — a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack,” she added.
Hassan, who is set to become chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in the next Congress, said AI safety legislation will be an early priority for the panel. She said one of the panel’s first hearings in the new year will focus on the risks AI poses to homeland security and critical infrastructure.
Hassan said the committee will “prioritize developing legislation to address these threats,” adding that she is exploring solutions such as requiring more rigorous safety testing before AI platforms publicly release models.
GAO did not issue recommendations in the report, which examined third-party products rather than its typical examination of federal agencies. Instead, GAO said it sought to highlight the risks for lawmakers and bring attention to safety concerns.

input.prompt: Publication date. Key findings: what bypass, which ChatGPT feature, numbers, OpenAI response.

response.result:
**Publication date:** November 5, 2026, by Alexey Bukhteyev of Check Point Research.

**Bypass:** The researchers found a way around ChatGPT's Lockdown Mode, which OpenAI describes as an optional setting that cuts off channels for outbound data leaks. The flaw let an attacker silently send chat data to an external server and display popups with arbitrary content inside the ChatGPT interface, enabling phishing and malware delivery.

**Feature involved:** The HTML page preview that OpenAI added to code blocks in February 2026. The HTML-preview sandbox used two nested iframes with the `allow-popups` and `allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox` permissions. ChatGPT overrode `window.open` to require user approval, but a popup opened through a nested iframe's `contentWindow.open` was not blocked.

**Numbers:** The article gives no user counts or similar metrics. Its dates are:
- February 2026: HTML page preview added.
- September 18, 2026: OpenAI deployed the fix.

**Severity notes:** In ChatGPT Classic (the Electron app), the researchers found `window.open` worked without a user gesture, so chat exfiltration could be zero-click. In browsers, victims could be lured through shared chats.

**OpenAI response:** The issue was responsibly disclosed. OpenAI removed the two popup permissions from the outer HTML-preview iframe. Check Point retested and confirmed the technique no longer works.

# LLMJacking: Summary of Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) / Mandiant Report

**Publication date:** November 2, 2026

## What LLMJacking Is

Threat actors hijack enterprise access to Large Language Model (LLM) services and run inference at the victim's expense. Unlike gradual cryptojacking, it can produce large billing spikes within hours.

## Key Figures

- **Single-day charges:** over $100,000 USD in some incidents
- **Cumulative charges:** up to $1 million USD before access was revoked
- **UNC6993:** over $100,000 USD in billing charges after gaining LLM API keys
- **Jet Night:** more than 500,000 LLM API calls in under 8 hours, passing nearly $1M in token costs to a victim
- **Jet Night pricing:** an unlimited plan at about $60/month, versus an estimated $100–$250/month market rate, which GTIG attributes to stolen keys

## Threat Actors and Campaigns

- **UNC6993:** Compromised a cloud instance via a misconfigured Service Account key. Also ran a session-hijacking page disguised as an application portal that tricked users into pasting raw JSON containing active access tokens, bypassing password and MFA.
- **"LLM Mixers":** Resellers that proxy and sell stolen LLM access. Access and monetization were split between separate clusters.
- **Jet Night (`jet-night.com`):** A token routing service likely built on stolen keys. It has advertised outages, probably from key revocations.
- **D1337-KAIROS persona:** Rebranded frontier-model endpoints, deployed a containerized backdoor using the Manus agent framework, and provisioned GPU instances across regions.
- **Custom relay (`ai-relay`):** Hosted on lookalike domains, including one that impersonated a victim's internal host, and fed the `newapi[.]pro` resale ecosystem.

## Initial Access Vectors

- Exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens: IAM credentials, Service Account keys, GitHub PATs, and session tokens
- Publicly exposed LLM endpoints (for example, Ollama `/api/create`)
- LLM API keys harvested from public GitHub repositories
- Federation tokens used to generate new access keys and bypass MFA

Validation sweeps used `max_tokens=1` requests to test stolen keys while evading EDR and SIEM volume alerts.

## CVE

- **CVE-2026-40217 (LiteLLM):** A user ID rebind flaw in the `/key/regenerate` endpoint lets standard Virtual Keys be elevated to `PROXY_ADMIN` master credentials.

## Tooling Mentioned

- Open-source: LiteLLM, new-api, gcli2api, SearXNG, agent-infra/sandbox, Manus
- Used for pooling stolen credentials, load-balancing, metering, and hiding request origins

## Detection Priorities

Treat unauthorized enablement of LLM services as a critical security event. Attackers often enable services first, then generate costs within minutes or hours.

**AWS (CloudTrail, `bedrock.amazonaws.com`):**
- Execution: `Converse`, `InvokeModel`, `InvokeModelWithResponseStream`
- Reconnaissance: `ListFoundationModels`, `ListInferenceProfiles`, `GetFoundationModelAvailability`
- Model unlocking: `PutUseCaseForModelAccess`, `CreateFoundationModelAgreement`
- Evasion: `DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration` and `PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration` from non-IaC principals (high severity)

**Azure (`Microsoft.CognitiveServices`):**
- Unauthorized deployments: `Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/deployments/write`
- Reconnaissance: `accounts/read`, `accounts/deployments/read`
- Evasion: `Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings/write` or `/delete`

**GCP (`aiplatform.googleapis.com`):**
- Service enablement: `google.api.serviceusage.v1.ServiceUsage.EnableService`
- Execution (requires Data Access logs, which are off by default): `PredictionService.Predict`, `GenerateContent`, `StreamGenerateContent`
- Reconnaissance: `ModelService.ListModels`, `EndpointService.ListEndpoints`, `PublisherModelService.ListPublisherModels`
- Evasion: `IAMPolicy.GetIamPolicy`, `ConfigServiceV2.ListSinks`, `GetSink`

## Mitigations

- **Credential hygiene:** Use a centralized secrets manager, rotate keys automatically, and scan code repositories for leaked secrets.
- **Least privilege:** Deny LLM service permissions unless explicitly required.
- **Phishing-resistant MFA** across identity providers and developer platforms.
- **Granular API key scopes:** Limit keys by model, environment, and usage, so a stolen utility-model key cannot call frontier models.
- **Spending caps and per-model quotas** to contain billing damage.
- **Gateway patching:** Keep LiteLLM and similar routers current (CVE-2026-40217).
- **Monitor for validation sweeps:** Alert on anomalous low-volume requests such as `max_tokens=1`.
- **Restrict model sources** to trusted internal or approved registries.
- **Shadow LLM discovery:** Use posture management tools to find unauthorized model endpoints.

## IOCs (Network)

| Indicator | Description |
|---|---|
| `jet-night.com` | LLM Mixer |
| `newapi.pro` | LLM Mixer |

Full IOCs are available in a GTI Collection for registered users.

# Fast Facts

Generative AI can drastically increase productivity and decrease the time it takes to perform many tasks. But AI could be misused to quickly develop sensitive knowledge and facilitate malicious acts.

In spring 2026, our prompts to four of the most used AI platforms—ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok—produced verified, feasible attacks that would cause harm to national security and the economy.

While the information wasn't new, the AI platforms were able to synthesize it into viable plans within hours, rather than weeks or months.

The word AI glowing on a computer circuit board

Skip to Highlights

# Highlights

# What GAO Found

In spring 2026, GAO’s prompts to four of the most used generative artificial intelligence (AI) platforms–Claude, Grok, ChatGPT, and Gemini—produced feasible information that could assist a malicious actor with planning and executing attacks. Specifically, in response to prompts, two platforms produced information for constructing and detonating an improvised explosive device (IED) designed to cause mass casualties. In addition, after prompting, two other platforms produced information for targeting the electrical grid with a drone and firearms, respectively, to cause economic harm. Each of these platforms provided detailed information that could be used to carry out attacks, such as specific targets, locations, timing, and attack methods. Each platform took less than 12 hours to generate the attack plans; however, the amount of time to get results could vary for many reasons, including the topic and user experience. In each case, GAO’s prompts triggered the platforms’ safeguards, such as denial, removal of information, or suspending accounts. GAO was able to circumvent those safeguards by using common safeguard-bypassing techniques. GAO verified the viability of the information through research, surveillance, and interviews with experts. The table provides details related to GAO’s tests.

# Why GAO Did This Study

Generative AI is dramatically increasing productivity and decreasing the time it takes to perform many tasks. These advancements are enabling malicious actors to pursue nefarious actions faster and more efficiently and empowering less-skilled individuals by filling knowledge gaps through providing detailed expertise in sensitive areas. There is a risk that generative AI could be misused to successfully complete malicious acts, such as producing harmful content, disclosing sensitive information, or carrying out other instructions that defy the AI’s intended purposes and built-in safeguards.

GAO was asked to review issues related to the malicious use of AI. This report describes how commercially available AI can be used for malicious purposes to exacerbate national security risks and cause economic harm.

To address this objective, through discussions with experts, GAO selected two scenarios in which AI could be used maliciously to: (1) facilitate the construction of an IED causing mass casualties and risks to national security and (2) facilitate an attack on the electrical grid causing economic harm. input.prompt: Publication date/time. Key facts: GAO report number, which models tested, exact findings and numbers, quotes, recommendations, vendor responses.

response.result:
**Publication:** Wednesday, November 18, 2026, 12:34 PM ET (Nextgov/FCW, by Grace Dille)

**Report:** GAO-27-108814, per the report link in the article. GAO published it Wednesday.

**Models tested:** ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok, during covert government testing in spring 2026. The report does not say which platform produced which output.

**Key findings:**
- All four platforms gave information that could help malicious actors plan attacks.
- Investigators bypassed safety guardrails using common techniques. GAO withheld the specific models and techniques to keep the tests from being recreated.
- Two attack types were covered: building and detonating a mass-casualty improvised explosive device, and targeting the electrical grid to cause economic damage.
- Outputs included specific targets, locations, timing, and attack methods.
- Each platform produced an attack plan in under 12 hours.
- GAO worked with experts, who verified that the information could be used to carry out the attacks.
- Platforms initially responded with refusals, content removal, or account suspensions, but these were circumvented.
- GAO says the findings are a point-in-time assessment and not "a statistically significant sample."

**Quotes:**
- Kevin Walsh, GAO director of IT and cybersecurity: "We got the nefarious information that we were after."
- Walsh: "These products are not fully in the control of the companies that are operating them."
- Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.), who requested the investigation: "the AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical."

**Recommendations:** None. GAO said it examined third-party products rather than federal agencies, and it aimed to alert lawmakers to the risks.

**Vendor responses:** Company officials generally said they will keep improving platform safety, according to the report. The article names Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceXAI, and does not give individual company statements.

**Next steps:** Hassan will chair the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee next Congress. She plans to make AI safety legislation an early priority, including possibly requiring more rigorous safety testing before public model releases.

results:
The search turned up coverage of a New York Times investigation into Megaspeed and Alibaba, but not the Times article itself. The details below come from secondary reports.

- **The core allegation:** The Times reported that Alibaba used Singapore venture Megaspeed and data centers in Malaysia to access over $4 billion in restricted Nvidia AI chips. One reported link is that the chips placed advanced computing hardware within reach of Zhejiang Lab, a research institute tied to China's military. Business Standard, which republished the Times piece, says whether Nvidia chips supplied by Megaspeed went from Alibaba to the lab is unclear.
- **Diversion and scale:** Megaspeed imported at least 136,000 Nvidia processors worth at least $4.6 billion, per Bloomberg, more than half were Blackwell chips, restricted from sale to China. Fortune adds that its government tallies ran 50,000 short, according to Bloomberg.
- **Export-control response:** On November 16, the US Commerce Department announced new export controls that name Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil as high-risk transshipment countries. Under the rules, overseas data centers that supply computing power above a set threshold to companies headquartered in China or other controlled countries must obtain a US export license within a set deadline. Separately, the Remote Access Security Act would give the Bureau of Industry and Security explicit authority to regulate remote access to controlled chips through cloud services, but it is a proposal, not an enacted rule.
- **Nvidia's position:** Huang said Nvidia "counted every one" of Megaspeed's deployments. Fortune also notes that 2 of 8 data centers Nvidia cited were absent Megaspeed hardware.
- **Context:** Atlantic Council notes that since 2023, Megaspeed has risen to become Nvidia's largest Southeast Asian buyer. Coverage also ties the story to a spy scandal involving former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, which has prompted federal smuggling probes.

Caveat: these are reports of allegations and investigations. Several links, such as whether the chips reached the lab, remain unconfirmed in the sources.

**Publication date:** November 10, 2026

**What was announced:** Google DeepMind introduced AlphaProof Code, an agentic framework for formal verification. Its researchers used it to formally verify the code of Signal's cryptographic protocol, which protects private messages in apps like Signal and Google Messages. The page calls this the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol "at this depth," and the first time such a protocol's implementation has been formally verified by any method. Human experts defined the security specifications and reviewed them. AI agents, powered by Gemini Carbon, wrote the proofs. The team also open-sourced its verification artifacts.

**Exact numbers:**
- Over 6 million lines of Lean code generated for the proofs
- About 1% of the codebase flagged for human review
- Four weeks for the verification process
- Two previously fixed bugs reintroduced into an isolated version of Signal's code; in both cases the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure

**Collaborators:**
- Authors: Pushmeet Kohli and Swarat Chaudhuri
- Research team: Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli

results:
The search turned up consistent coverage of the clearance, announced November 13, 2026, though the details below come from trade press and the companies' release, not the FDA database.

- **What was cleared:** Bracco and Avicenna.AI received 510(k) clearance for UPTUNITY | Aneurysm. The software is a CADe/CADx tool that flags suspected saccular brain aneurysms above 3 mm on head CTA images ([diagnosticimaging.com](https://www.diagnosticimaging.com/view/fda-cta-based-ai-software-brain-aneurysm-detection-follow-up)).
- **Product scope:** It is the first product in Bracco's new UPTUNITY line of interpretive AI ([auntminnie.com](https://www.auntminnie.com/imaging-informatics/artificial-intelligence/news/16425547/bracco-diagnostics-inc-bracco-avicennaai-get-fda-clearance-for-brain-aneurysm-ai-software)). Its follow-up function, which compares exams over time, is slated for the RSNA meeting ([diagnosticimaging.com](https://www.diagnosticimaging.com/view/fda-cta-based-ai-software-brain-aneurysm-detection-follow-up)).
- **Commercial roles:** Avicenna.AI will lead U.S. promotion and distribution. The companies say the product is meant for use by trained specialists, with physicians keeping control of decisions ([appliedradiology.com](https://www.appliedradiology.com/news/bracco-and-avicenna-ai-introduce-ai-enabled-uptunitytm-for-aneurysm-detection)).
- **Clearance numbers:** The release ties the clearance to K262062 and K262147 ([appliedradiology.com](https://www.appliedradiology.com/news/bracco-and-avicenna-ai-introduce-ai-enabled-uptunitytm-for-aneurysm-detection)). One analysis says the FDA's public record lists October 19, 2026 as the decision date for CINA-Aneurysm+, which is earlier than the announcement ([techedgeai.com](https://techedgeai.com/?p=43856)).
- **Caveat on wording:** One outlet notes that 510(k) clearance is a different pathway from premarket approval and should not be described as FDA approval ([techedgeai.com](https://techedgeai.com/?p=43856)).

I didn't find the original Cision/PR Newswire release or the FDA 510(k) summaries directly, so those should be checked before relying on specifics.

# Nvidia created a weird bit of intrigue by not filing a routine SEC report

Julie Bort

1:57 PM PST · November 18, 2026

During Nvidia’s quarterly call on Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim-CEO Colette Kress dropped this little oddity: She said Nvidia wouldn’t be immediately filing its quarterly results report, known as a 10-Q, with the SEC. “We plan to file our 10-Q in the coming weeks.” And she offered no reason why.

The delay was widely noticed. Among the many comments on X about it , economic and investment analyst Edward Dowd called it a “red flag.” Nvidia has typically filed the 10-Q the same day it reports results.

The 10-Q offers far more detail about a company’s operations than an earnings press release, including sections that disclose “legal proceedings,” which include lawsuits that could affect the company; and “risk factors,” which cover other potentially business-impairing items.

The announcement of the delay was so unusual that UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri asked about it after the public earnings call. Nvidia told him the delay was related to whether the company would need to disclose additional information about its ongoing investigation into Huang in the 10-Q.

“The company announced that the 10-Q will be filed ‘in the coming weeks’ – later than usual. When queried on our callback, management indicated this was related to the ongoing investigation and whether any additional risk factors would need to be added to the filing,” Arcuri wrote in his research note. (Arcuri still rates the stock a “buy” by the way, although he did lower his price target to $220 from $240. The stock is now trading around $150).

Notably, on the same day that Nvidia reported earnings, The Wall Street Journal reported that the SEC is investigating Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors.

So the mystery thickens: What will Nvidia disclose? We’ll have to wait and see. (Nvidia has not yet responded to our request for comment.)

The delay suggests the company may have more to say about its mounting legal troubles. Nvidia is now facing multiple federal investigations over allegations that its partners were selling restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. So far, the scrutiny has come from a number of congressional committees ; the Department of Justice looking into Megaspeed , the company run by a woman with whom Huang had an affair and who is also suspected of being a Chinese spy; and now, reportedly, the SEC.

Additionally, Nvidia is conducting its own internal investigation into Huang after he admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang (the Megaspeed executive), and allegations surfaced that he also had affairs with other Nvidia employees.

There’s little doubt that Wall Street will scrutinize that 10-Q once it’s finally filed. The intrigue brings to mind the old saying: “Doctors bury their mistakes. Lawyers put theirs in prison. And accountants hide theirs in the footnotes.”

# Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explains why he asked 60K employees to quit

Julie Bort

4:42 PM PST · November 18, 2026

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained Wednesday why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit instead of reducing the workforce via another massive layoff.

Short answer: AI, but not, he insists, in the way you might expect. He’s not saying he’s replacing employees with AI, especially software engineers. He’s saying he’s reorganizing Microsoft into a company where everyone uses AI to do their work, and their jobs become focused on managing that AI.

The buyout was “to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices,” he told Andrew Ross Sorkin during the DealBook Summit.

“Let’s take software engineering. We went from, ‘Well, we don’t buy that AI can ever do software.’ To suddenly, ‘Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?’ To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point,” he explained.

For some people, “that reorganization and change is sort of hard, right?” he added, “but, I mean, it has to be done.”

He offered the example of the team that builds Cowork, the AI agent in Microsoft 365 apps. He said the team consists of just 11 developers who have mastered using AI to do their jobs. “They build a software factory that builds the product. They don’t build the product.”

He believes that every employee will one day similarly become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work. “That level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs.”

But Microsoft, as a 51-year-old company, didn’t grow up as an AI-first company. “So the question is, how quickly can an incumbent transform the work, the workflow, and the work artifact, and with all the wage support that goes with it?” he said. “It’s going to take a bit more time than anyone expects. And there is going to be in all of this, you know, people who may say, ‘Hey, I have some other choices I want to make.’”

When asked about this same topic — why ask 60,000 people to voluntarily resign — last week by Gergely Orosz on his The Pragmatic Engineer podcast , Nadella further explained, “We have created enormous anxiety in people sort of feeling that they don’t have control of their own destiny because the way we have talked about this AI revolution.”

He called out talk about the singularity (the hypothetical point at which AI surpasses human intelligence) and predictions that AI will take away all jobs. “All of that leads anyone who even wants to change to be sort of anxious … You have to sort of walk the hard walk of really making the structural changes, getting people slotted, giving them opportunity.”

In other words, the buyout was the message to employees: You can get with the new AI-first program, which will radically change your job, or you choose to get on with your life. Elsewhere.

results:
The Bloomberg story from November 19, 2026 reports that Alphabet's chief investment officer is calling for local job investment in response to opposition. Other coverage fills in the details of the pledge and the backlash behind it.

- **The pledge:** Google plans to spend $1 billion on local programs in data-center communities by the end of 2027 and to pay full real-property taxes on new campuses. It also plans to stop using nondisclosure agreements with state and local governments, with limited exceptions. (Google will spend $1 billion on local programs in data-center communities by end of 2027 and pay full property taxes on new campuses.)
- **The backlash:** Coverage ties the pledge to November's local votes. Data-center limits passed in 40 of 41 US ballot measures across 10 states, according to unofficial counts. (Local limits on data centers passed in 40 of 41 US ballot measures across 10 states, including 14 Ohio towns.)
- **Porat's admission:** Semafor reports she conceded that Google and other AI companies have not convinced US voters the spending is worth it. She said she is hearing voters' affordability concerns firsthand. ("I've been traveling the country quite a bit and the pain you saw reflected in polls, I'm hearing firsthand around affordability," Porat told Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World.)
- **Earlier framing:** In June, Porat called data centers a "job creator" and argued that for every job at Google's own data centers, third parties create nine more. (For every job a company like Google creates at its own data centers, third parties create nine additional jobs, she adds.)
- **Financial context:** Google expects up to $205 billion in capital expenditures this year, and Porat said 2027 spending will be higher still. (Google expects to spend up to $205 billion on capital expenditures this year, and Alphabet's longtime investment chief Ruth Porat told Semafor that 2027 will be higher still.)

results:
Google has pledged to spend $1 billion on local programs in data-center communities and to change how it handles taxes, disclosure, and NDAs. The main points, with the most recent coverage first:

- **Spending:** In the United States through the end of 2027, Google expects to invest $1 billion in locally tailored programs in data center communities, according to the company's own page.
- **Taxes:** Google says it will pay full real property taxes on new campuses. The company argues this gives local communities a long-term, predictable revenue stream for services like firefighters, teachers, and parks.
- **NDAs:** Google says it will stop using nondisclosure agreements with state and local governments, with limited exceptions for trade secrets or operational security.
- **Disclosure and utilities:** It plans to disclose its role by its first project application or public meeting and publish some project-level information on water, sound, light and traffic. It will also cover the electricity its data centers use and their direct grid-connection costs.

**Context:** Coverage ties the pledge to local opposition. One report says voters sided against data center development in 40 of 41 ballot measures across 10 states. Reporting also notes that Meta and Amazon said recently they will each spend $1 billion on financial incentives to host communities. Separately, Senate Democrats criticized Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft for using NDAs to keep the public out.

**Open question:** One outlet asks whether the $1 billion will reach rural Ohio towns that already voted to limit expansion, or only communities still open to new builds. The sources I found don't answer that, and the pledge is framed as an expectation rather than a binding commitment.

# Anthropic prices IPO at $83 a share, above projected range

Marina Temkin

2:11 PM PST · November 18, 2026

Anthropic has priced its long-awaited IPO at $83 per share , above its initial range of $70 to $78, signaling strong investor appetite for one of the companies at the center of the AI boom, despite market jitters following the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which shook confidence in the industry. The Claude maker sold 980 million shares in the offering, up from the 825 million initially planned, generating $81.3 billion in proceeds and surpassing SpaceX’s $75 billion record to become the largest IPO in history by proceeds raised.

At the IPO price, Anthropic is valued at roughly $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, a significant increase from the $965 billion the company reached in May when it raised $65 billion in its last private market round , but below the $2 trillion it was reportedly aiming for several months ago.

Anthropic will begin its life as a public company on Thursday, trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” A strong first day of trading would signal that investors remain optimistic about AI adoption, despite recent volatility in AI-driven stocks.

The company’s performance is expected to set expectations for private AI companies, including Anthropic’s main rival OpenAI, which was last reportedly valued at $1.25 billion but has yet to announce plans for an IPO.

Although none of Anthropic’s venture capital investors holds more than a 5% stake in the company, the IPO is a massive windfall for its numerous backers . Investors who own approximately 1% of the company reportedly include Sequoia, as well as former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC also holds about a 1% stake in the company, according to a person familiar with the matter. Other backers set to make billions are Iconiq, Menlo Ventures, Coatue, and Sound Ventures, a firm launched by Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher. Spark Capital, the only VC firm known to hold a board seat at the company (it was the first institutional investor in the company, leading its $450 million Series C round in 2023 that valued the company at $4.5 billion), also stands to make a fortune off its early investment in Anthropic.

Some of the Anthropic’s existing investors, namely Sequoia, Iconiq, Lightspeed, Accel, and Altimeter Capital Management, are so enthusiastic about Anthropic’s future that they are reportedly planning to buy billions of dollars’ worth of the company’s shares in the IPO.

Yet the investors’ holdings in Anthropic pale in comparison to those of the company’s strategic partners Amazon, which owns nearly 15% of the company, and Google, which holds almost 14%. A group of major tech companies, including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners, have also agreed to purchase $26 billion worth of non-voting shares through a private placement alongside the IPO.

The company’s seven co-founders , including CEO Dario Amodei, each sold nearly 3.4 million shares in the IPO, according to the S-1 filing, bringing in about $282 million for each.

This post has been updated with the number of shares sold and IPO proceeds.
